domains.name: Lecture & Academic Listening
domains.summary: Academic listening is modelled here as two interacting sets of processes: decoding, which turns the acoustic signal into words and clauses in real time, and meaning-building, which relates what has been decoded to context, discourse structure, speaker purpose and prior knowledge. The domain moves from perceptual topics (connected speech, segmentation, speech rate, accent) through lecture discourse (phases, organisational and relevance markers, main points, stance) to the settings in which students listen (live and recorded lectures, seminars, briefings, academic media), with metacognitive strategy running throughout. Listening is treated as something to be taught, not only tested, and accent variation is treated as normal in international universities rather than as deviation from a single native-speaker norm. Deaf and hard-of-hearing students, and others who rely on captions, transcripts or note-taking support, may show these skills through other modes, and tasks should allow for this.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why natural speech can be hard to catch and practical ways to follow the structure, key points and viewpoints of lectures, seminars and recorded talks.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build decoding of connected speech and confidence with short, clearly signposted lecture extracts on accessible content, together with simple preparation routines.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Move from short decoding work to full-length authentic lectures on first-year content, with explicit work on discourse and relevance markers and main-point selection, assessed through lecture notes and listening-into-writing tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume basic lecture decoding and work with dense, discipline-related lectures and recorded seminars, focusing on relevance marking, speaker stance on contested material and following peer discussion.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Use students' own module lectures and recordings to diagnose specific decoding or discourse problems and build independent review strategies.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on dense, fast-paced specialist lectures, seminar discussion among peers from many language backgrounds, and inferring lecturer stance on contested material.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address research seminars, conference talks, podcasts and multi-party discussion, where speakers are specialists with varied accents who signpost less explicitly.

domains.name: Note-taking & Note-making
domains.summary: The domain treats note-taking (recording from lectures in real time) and note-making (building notes from reading and from later review) as distinct but connected practices. Following Kiewra (1985), notes serve both an encoding function, through the processing involved in taking them, and an external-storage function for later review, and the review function often matters more; the domain therefore covers selection, shorthand and format, lecture and reading notes, review, digital tools and collaboration. Claims about particular formats, or about longhand versus laptop notes, are presented with their evidential limits.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to take notes that capture the key ideas of lectures and readings, record where each idea came from, and use your notes to revise and write.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish selection, abbreviation and simple formats with short, well-structured inputs, and link notes from reading to avoiding unintentional plagiarism.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Develop real-time lecture notes with explicit selection criteria and formats, and source-tracked reading notes, feeding integrated listening- and reading-into-writing assessments.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Concentrate on source-tracked notes from longer, multiple readings that separate quotation, paraphrase and comment and are organised by theme to feed synthesis and the extended project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work with students' own lecture and reading notes, focusing on review through self-testing and on informed choices of tools.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Manage heavy reading loads with source-tracked, thematically organised notes that support synthesis and the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Note-making shifts towards literature management and research records; reading notes that keep source and own words strictly apart remain central.

domains.name: Pronunciation & Fluency
domains.summary: The domain adopts the intelligibility principle (Levis, 2005): the goal is speech that listeners can understand with reasonable effort, not a native-like accent. Building on Munro and Derwing's (1995) distinction between accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility, priority goes to the features most likely to affect understanding in academic speaking — word stress in academic vocabulary, thought groups and prominence, intonation for discourse functions, high-functional-load segmentals — together with fluency and repair. Pronunciation is linked to listening, since perception supports production, and to the presentations, seminars and teaching in which students use it; accent is treated as part of speakers' identity rather than as an error to be removed. Listeners share responsibility for understanding, so assessment should judge intelligibility rather than accentedness, and speakers who stammer or have other speech differences should not be assessed against fluency norms they cannot meet.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn which features of pronunciation most affect whether listeners understand you, and practise them in presentations and seminars. Your goal is to be understood, not to change your accent.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish intelligibility as the goal, with focused work on word stress, thought groups and each learner's own highest-priority sounds.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Integrate word stress, thought groups and prominence with presentation and seminar speaking, using recordings, listener transcription and peer feedback to set individual goals.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Apply prominence, intonation and technical-term pronunciation to explaining specialist content and data in presentations and seminars, preparing for postgraduate presenting and, for some, teaching.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Provide short, targeted support for assessed presentations and technical vocabulary, usually through individual feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on specialist terms, numbers and data in speech, and on fluent delivery of dense content within strict time limits.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support conference presentations, vivas and teaching (for example as graduate teaching assistants), where prosody affects how clearly explanations come across to audiences.

topics.name: Listening processes: decoding and meaning-building
topics.description: Understand listening as the real-time interaction of decoding processes (perceiving sounds and syllables, recognising words, parsing clauses) and meaning-building processes (enriching what is decoded with context, background knowledge and discourse structure, and deciding what matters). The distinction lets learners and teachers locate where comprehension breaks down instead of treating 'I didn't understand' as a single problem with a single remedy.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes, with examples from their own listening, a decoding failure (not recognising in speech a word they know in writing) from a meaning-building failure (recognising the words but missing the point)
Explains why listening differs from reading: the signal is transient, word boundaries are not marked and the listener does not control the pace
Explains how using context and prediction can compensate for decoding gaps but can also produce confident misinterpretation
Classifies entries in a listening log as decoding or meaning-building problems and proposes a different kind of practice for each
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 30-second unscripted lecture extract twice and ask the learner to write down exactly what they heard and then say in one sentence what the speaker meant. Compare both with the original: note whether errors arise at word level (decoding) or in interpretation (meaning-building). Then ask the learner to classify their own errors and check whether their classification matches yours.

topics.name: Recognising connected speech
topics.description: Recognise words whose form in natural speech differs from their citation form because of weak forms, elision, assimilation, linking and other reductions, which affect function words and frequent phrases most. Without this, learners fail to recognise words they already know in writing, and a few missed function words can make a whole clause impossible to parse.
masteryEvidence: Recognises weak forms of common function words (of, to, and, can, have, them) in unscripted academic speech
Restores the full written form of reduced sequences (going to, want to, would have, what do you) when transcribing short extracts
Maps elided and assimilated forms in frequent sequences (next point, would you, in particular) to the words they represent
Resegments linked sequences in which a final consonant attaches to a following vowel
Transcribes a 15-second extract of lecture speech with function words largely intact
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play five short sentences taken from authentic lecture speech, each containing weak forms and linking (for example a sentence with 'some of them' or 'what we want to do is'), once each at natural speed. Ask the learner to write every word. Check whether function words and reduced sequences are restored, not just content words, and whether errors cluster on particular reduction types.

topics.name: Segmenting the speech stream
topics.description: Identify where words begin and end in continuous speech, using strong syllables (syllables with full, unreduced vowels, including those carrying primary stress), which in English mark the start of most content words, together with lexical knowledge, grammar and context to confirm or revise a hypothesis. Segmentation errors (hearing 'a notion' as 'an ocean') produce misrecognitions that then mislead interpretation of the rest of the utterance.
masteryEvidence: Uses strong syllables (those with full vowels, including stressed syllables) as anchors to locate the probable onset of content words in an unfamiliar stretch of speech
Detects and corrects a segmentation error when the first interpretation does not fit the grammar or context
Separates multi-word sequences heard as a single unit into their component words
Recognises words that begin with a weak syllable (consider, analysis, economy) as a frequent source of boundary errors and checks them deliberately
Explains how linking across word boundaries can produce alternative segmentations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play eight short phrases from lectures that contain ambiguous boundaries (for example 'a notion' versus 'an ocean', or a weak-initial academic word preceded by an article) and ask the learner to write each phrase. Replay any errors once. Check whether boundaries are placed correctly and whether the learner revises an implausible segmentation on the second hearing and can say what cue led to the revision.

topics.name: Coping with natural speech rate
topics.description: Follow lectures and discussion delivered at natural, unscripted rates by building automatic word recognition through repeated exposure and by using compensatory strategies (continuing past gaps, using restatement and redundancy, prioritising) when decoding falls behind. A sense that speech is 'too fast' often reflects decoding that is not yet automatic rather than simply the speaker's rate.
masteryEvidence: Continues to follow an extended extract after missing a word or phrase instead of stopping to work out the gap
Recovers content missed on first mention from later restatement, examples or summaries
Shows improved transcription or summary accuracy for a speaker after repeated exposure to that speaker
Selects practice material and playback speed appropriately and increases speed as recognition improves
Distinguishes, when reflecting on a difficult lecture, between a speaker's rate and their own decoding load
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 2-minute unscripted lecture extract at natural speed and ask for a short summary, then play a section of it at 0.75 speed and ask the learner what they now catch that they missed. If comprehension improves sharply at reduced speed, decoding automaticity is the main issue. Check also whether the learner kept following after a missed segment or lost the thread entirely.

topics.name: Understanding varied accents
topics.description: Adapt to the range of accents used by lecturers, supervisors and peers in international universities, including regional varieties from countries where English is the majority language and the many accents of English used as a lingua franca. Comprehension of an unfamiliar accent typically improves with exposure, and treating varied accents as normal rather than as departures from one standard is part of listening competence and of participating on equal terms.
masteryEvidence: Shows improved comprehension of an initially unfamiliar accent after several minutes of exposure, measured by transcription or summary accuracy
Identifies specific features of a speaker's accent that caused misrecognition (for example vowel quality or stress placement) and adjusts expectations
Seeks out recordings by speakers with a range of accents for independent listening
Describes accent variation among lecturers and peers without equating a regional, second-language or unfamiliar accent with low competence
Uses clarification and confirmation checks when a peer's accent blocks understanding in discussion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play two short extracts on similar content, one by a speaker whose accent is familiar to the learner and one by a speaker whose accent is not, and ask for the key points of each. Then play a further 2 minutes by the unfamiliar speaker and ask for the key points of a new section. Check whether comprehension of the unfamiliar speaker improves with exposure and whether the learner can say what caused the initial difficulty.

topics.name: Metacognitive listening strategies
topics.description: Plan for, monitor, solve problems during and evaluate listening, drawing on knowledge of oneself as a listener, of the demands of listening tasks and of the strategies available. Metacognitive regulation lets learners direct their own listening development beyond the classroom, but it complements rather than replaces practice in decoding.
masteryEvidence: Sets a listening goal and predicts content and vocabulary before a listening task
Notices comprehension breakdowns while listening and chooses a response (continue, infer and verify later, mark for replay)
Verifies predictions and inferences against what was actually said on a second listening
Evaluates after listening which strategies helped and why, with reference to specific moments
Keeps a listening log that records problems, strategies tried and changes over time
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a listening task, ask the learner to talk through what they did before, during and after listening. Check whether they describe planning, monitoring and evaluation, and whether strategies are linked to specific problems ('I lost the word after the example, so I listened for the summary') rather than generic statements ('I listened carefully').

topics.name: Preparing for lectures
topics.description: Prepare for a lecture by previewing slides, module outlines and set readings, activating and building relevant background knowledge, predicting content and organisation, and pre-learning key terms including how they sound. Preparation can reduce real-time processing load so that more attention is available for following the argument, provided predictions are checked rather than trusted.
masteryEvidence: Lists likely topics and key terms for a lecture from its slides, module outline and set reading
Checks the pronunciation as well as the meaning of key technical terms before the lecture
Writes predictions or questions in advance and checks them during or after the lecture
Sets up a note frame based on the predicted structure
Adjusts their preparation routine after evaluating which steps helped
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the title and slides of a lecture they have not yet heard and 15 minutes to prepare. Ask them to show what they produced (term list, predictions, note frame). After the lecture, check whether the preparation was used, whether predicted terms were recognised aurally, and whether the learner noticed where the lecture departed from their predictions.

topics.name: Lecture structure and phases
topics.description: Recognise the recurring phases of university lectures — discourse structuring (previewing, reviewing, moving on), content, exemplification, conclusion, evaluation and interaction — and that these phases interleave and recur rather than following a fixed sequence. Knowing the typical shape of a lecture lets listeners anticipate what kind of information is coming and allocate attention accordingly.
masteryEvidence: Identifies discourse-structuring phases (preview, review, transition) in a lecture recording and states their function
Distinguishes content phases from exemplification and evaluation phases in an extract
Uses the lecture's opening preview to predict the sequence of topics and notices when the plan changes
Recognises interaction phases (questions to the audience, pair tasks, polls) as part of the lecture rather than as interruptions
Describes how a lecturer's delivery style (closely scripted, conversational, highly interactive) affects how explicitly structure is signalled
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 10-minute lecture recording and a blank timeline. Ask them to mark where the lecturer previews, moves to a new topic, gives an example, evaluates, summarises and interacts with the audience. Compare with your own analysis, checking especially whether structuring talk is distinguished from content and whether recurring structuring phases are noticed.

topics.name: Lecture discourse markers
topics.description: Recognise the macro-markers that signal a lecture's larger organisation (what I want to do today is…, let's turn now to…) and the micro-markers that segment and link ideas locally (so, now, right, OK, and then), and use them in real time to track where the lecture is and predict what comes next. Spoken markers are often unstressed and reduced, and organisation is also signalled by pausing and pitch, so recognising structure is partly a decoding task.
masteryEvidence: Identifies macro-markers that announce, sequence, conclude or return to topics in an authentic lecture
Distinguishes organisational uses of so, now, right and OK from their other meanings
Predicts, on hearing a marker, what kind of content follows (a new topic, an example, a summary, a return)
Recognises section boundaries signalled mainly by pause, pitch reset or change of pace when lexical markers are absent
Structures notes with headings that correspond to the macro-markers used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 5-minute lecture extract and ask the learner to write down every phrase that told them where the lecture was going, with what each signalled. Check whether macro-markers are caught, whether functions are correctly identified, whether informal markers (so, right, what we're going to do) are noticed, and whether any boundary marked only prosodically is detected.

topics.name: Emphasis and relevance markers
topics.description: Recognise the lexicogrammatical and prosodic means by which lecturers flag what matters: imperatives (remember that…, note that…), evaluative nouns and adjectives (the key point, crucially), explicit references to assessment, and emphatic stress, slowing, pausing and repetition. Relevance markers also flag content as less important (you don't need to know the details), so they guide what listeners prioritise, note and review.
masteryEvidence: Identifies verbal relevance markers in an authentic lecture and the content each one flags
Recognises prosodic emphasis (heavy stress, slowing, pausing, repetition) as a signal of importance when no verbal marker is present
Distinguishes markers that raise the importance of content from those that lower it
Recognises references to examinations or assignments as relevance signals
Marks flagged content visually in notes and prioritises it in review
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 10-minute lecture section in which three or four points are flagged as important, verbally or prosodically, and one is flagged as unimportant. Afterwards, ask the learner which points the lecturer most wanted students to remember and how they knew. Check whether flagged points are retrieved, whether the downgraded point is treated as such, and whether the learner can name the cue.

topics.name: Identifying main points and supporting detail
topics.description: Select the central claims, concepts and organising points of an extended stretch of academic speech and distinguish them from elaboration, examples, evidence and restatement, in real time and without the option of re-reading. This selection underpins lecture note-taking, oral summaries and integrated listening-to-writing tasks.
masteryEvidence: States the main point of a 5–10-minute lecture section in one or two sentences that the lecturer would accept as accurate
Distinguishes a claim from the example or evidence offered for it
Reconstructs the hierarchy of a lecture section (main point, sub-points, examples) from notes
Uses previews, summaries and relevance markers to confirm what was central
Identifies a point that is built up across several minutes rather than stated once
topics.assessmentPrompt: After a 10-minute lecture section, ask the learner to write the three main points in order of importance and one example or piece of evidence for each. Check against your own analysis whether the points are central rather than salient details, and whether each example is attached to the point it actually supports.

topics.name: Handling digressions and asides
topics.description: Recognise when a lecturer departs from the main thread — for an anecdote, joke, personal aside, administrative notice or tangential example — judge whether the departure illustrates a main point or is incidental, and recognise the return to the topic. This stops learners mistaking asides for core content or losing the thread altogether.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the start and end of a digression in an authentic lecture recording
Recognises markers of return (anyway, so, back to…, where was I) and reorients notes accordingly
Judges whether an anecdote or aside illustrates a main point and, if so, which one
Recognises humour or irony in an aside and does not record it as a literal claim
Keeps notes on the main thread coherent across a digression
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play an authentic lecture extract containing an anecdote or aside of about a minute. Ask the learner to summarise the main thread and say whether and how the aside related to it. Check whether the aside is presented as a main point, whether the return to the topic was recognised, and whether any illustrative function was understood.

topics.name: Inferring speaker stance
topics.description: Infer a lecturer's or speaker's evaluation of the ideas they present — endorsement, scepticism, criticism, irony, degree of certainty — from stance expressions, hedges and boosters, the framing of reported views, and prosody, and distinguish the speaker's own position from positions they report. This matters most where lectures present contested theories and evidence rather than settled facts.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes in a lecture extract between views the speaker reports and views the speaker endorses
Identifies the degree of certainty a speaker attaches to a claim from hedges, boosters and modal expressions
Recognises evaluative prosody (for example a doubtful or ironic delivery) and its effect on the literal meaning
States the speaker's overall position after a section presenting several views, citing the cues that reveal it
Annotates notes to show the speaker's evaluation of each reported position
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a lecture extract in which the speaker presents two or three positions and evaluates them, including one hedged evaluation and one sceptical or ironic one. Ask the learner what the speaker thinks of each and how they know. Check whether reported views are confused with the speaker's own, whether degrees of certainty are captured, and whether prosodic cues are used.

topics.name: Following multi-party discussion
topics.description: Follow seminar, tutorial and group discussions by tracking who is speaking, what position each participant takes, how each contribution responds to earlier ones, and where the discussion has reached, despite overlapping talk, varied accents and little explicit signposting. Following the discussion is a precondition for contributing relevantly to it.
masteryEvidence: Summarises the positions taken by different participants in a recorded seminar extract
Identifies how a contribution relates to an earlier one (agreement, challenge, extension, change of topic)
Tracks the current focus of a discussion and recognises when it shifts
Checks a peer's point by paraphrase or confirmation question before responding to it
Follows discussion in which speakers have varied accents and some overlapping talk
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 5-minute recording of an authentic or realistic seminar with four participants. Ask the learner to map who said what and how each contribution related to the one before. Check accuracy of attribution and whether relationships (agree, challenge, extend, ask) are correctly identified, especially where they are implicit.

topics.name: Integrating slides, visuals and speech
topics.description: Coordinate attention between the lecturer's speech and what is shown — slides, diagrams, data displays, equations, demonstrations, board work — resolving spoken references to visuals (this curve here, as you can see) and integrating the two channels rather than reading slides at the expense of listening. Lecture content is often distributed across modes, so neither channel alone is sufficient.
masteryEvidence: Resolves spoken deictic references to the correct element of a slide or diagram
Identifies information given in speech that is not on the slide, and vice versa
Annotates printed or digital slides with spoken additions instead of copying slide text
Follows a spoken explanation of a graph or diagram, identifying the feature discussed at each point
Shifts attention from slide to speaker when the lecturer signals a key point orally
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 5-minute recorded lecture segment with slides and give the learner a printout of the slides. Ask them to annotate the slides with what the lecturer added orally. Check whether annotations capture spoken-only content and whether spoken references are linked to the right slide elements.

topics.name: Using lecture capture strategically
topics.description: Use lecture recordings, automatic captions and transcripts as targeted review and repair tools — replaying sections marked as difficult, checking key terms and completing notes — rather than as a substitute for attending or a reason to rewatch whole lectures passively. Strategic use depends on knowing what was missed and why.
masteryEvidence: Marks moments of difficulty during a live lecture so that specific sections can be replayed later
Checks spellings and pronunciation of unfamiliar terms using captions or transcripts, verifying automatic captions against slides or readings
Completes and corrects notes from a recording within a planned time limit
Plans use of recordings within a weekly study schedule instead of deferring listening
Explains the risks of substituting recordings for attendance and of passive rewatching
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show their notes from a recent lecture and describe how, if at all, they used the recording afterwards. Check for targeted replay (marked gaps, timestamps) rather than whole-lecture rewatching or no use, and whether automatic captions were checked against other sources for technical terms.

topics.name: Understanding spoken instructions and briefings
topics.description: Understand spoken instructions, assignment briefings, laboratory and fieldwork safety briefings and administrative announcements well enough to act on them correctly, attending to sequence, conditions, deadlines and the strength of obligation, and checking understanding against written sources. Errors here have direct practical, safety and assessment consequences.
masteryEvidence: Records the steps, deadlines and requirements of a spoken assignment briefing accurately
Distinguishes obligatory from optional actions in spoken instructions, including obligations expressed indirectly (I'd like you to…, you'll want to…)
Follows a multi-step spoken procedure in the correct sequence, for example in a laboratory demonstration
Asks targeted clarification questions about conditions, deadlines or formats
Checks spoken announcements against written sources such as the learning platform or course handbook
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 2-minute assignment briefing that includes a deadline, a word limit, a submission method, one obligatory element expressed indirectly and one genuinely optional element. Ask the learner to write a checklist. Check whether all requirements are captured and whether the indirect obligation and the option are correctly distinguished.

topics.name: Listening to academic media
topics.description: Use academic podcasts, recorded conference talks, public lectures and documentaries as sources of knowledge: judging their credibility, following conversational, interview and panel formats that are less structured than lectures, extracting content relevant to a purpose, and recording details (speaker, date, platform, timestamps) so the material can be cited. Such media are increasingly set as course materials and used for independent study.
masteryEvidence: Evaluates the credibility of an academic podcast or recorded talk (speaker expertise, affiliation, evidence cited) before using it as a source
Extracts the points relevant to an assignment question from a 20-minute podcast or talk
Follows interview and panel formats, attributing points to the right speaker
Records citation details including timestamps for paraphrased or quoted points
Uses playback controls, chapter markers and transcripts efficiently to locate content
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an assignment question and a 20-minute academic podcast or talk. Ask for notes on content relevant to the question, with timestamps, and a two-sentence judgement of the source's credibility. Check the relevance of what was selected, the accuracy of timestamps and attribution, and the basis of the credibility judgement.

topics.name: Functions of notes
topics.description: Understand that notes serve two functions: taking them can promote encoding, as the note-taker selects, condenses and connects ideas, and the notes themselves are an external store for later review. Research suggests the review function often contributes more to learning, so notes must be complete and usable later, and the way they are taken affects how much processing occurs.
masteryEvidence: Explains the difference between the encoding and external-storage functions of notes with reference to their own practice
Evaluates a set of notes for whether they could support revision a month later
Explains why near-verbatim transcription tends to involve less processing than condensing ideas in one's own words
Relates decisions about note-taking (amount, wording, format) to how the notes will later be used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner two sets of notes on the same lecture, one near-verbatim and fragmentary, the other selective and organised. Ask which would be more useful for revision a month later and why. Check whether the answer refers both to the processing involved in taking the notes and to their usability as a record.

topics.name: Selecting what to note
topics.description: Decide what to record — main ideas and the relationships between them, key terms and definitions, essential examples and evidence, and the sources mentioned — rather than attempting to transcribe, adjusting the selection to the purpose the notes will serve. Selection is the central intellectual act of note-taking and depends on recognising the structure and priorities of the input.
masteryEvidence: Records main ideas and the relationships between them in condensed form rather than in full sentences
Includes key terms, definitions and representative examples while omitting repetition and redundancy
Adjusts what is recorded to a stated purpose, for example noting methods in detail for an assignment on methodology
Records the sources and authors a lecturer or text refers to
Produces notes in which the hierarchy of ideas (main point, sub-points, examples) is visible
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a 400-word text or 4-minute lecture extract and a stated purpose (for example, notes for an essay on the causes of a phenomenon). Allow 5 minutes for notes. Check the proportion of main ideas to detail, the relevance of what is recorded to the purpose, and whether the hierarchy of ideas is visible.

topics.name: Abbreviations and symbols
topics.description: Use conventional abbreviations and symbols (e.g., i.e., cf., →, ∴, ≠, ↑, ≈) and a consistent personal shorthand, including abbreviations for recurrent subject terms, to record quickly while keeping notes decodable later. Symbols for logical relations (cause, consequence, contrast, change) let notes preserve reasoning rather than just topics.
masteryEvidence: Uses a consistent set of symbols for logical relations (cause, consequence, contrast, increase, decrease, approximation)
Creates abbreviations for recurrent subject terms and records them in a key
Decodes their own notes accurately a week after writing them
Avoids shorthand so idiosyncratic or ambiguous that meaning is lost
Uses conventional Latin abbreviations (e.g., i.e., cf.) with their correct meanings
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to take notes on a short lecture extract, then two days later to rewrite one section in full sentences using only the notes. Check whether symbols for relations are used consistently and whether the rewritten section recovers the meaning, including the logical relations, accurately.

topics.name: Note formats
topics.description: Choose and use note formats — indented linear outlines, Cornell-style pages with cue and summary areas, concept or mind maps, tables and matrices, flow diagrams — according to the structure of the input and the use the notes will serve. Format choice can make visible relationships that linear transcription obscures, but no single format is best for all purposes.
masteryEvidence: Matches format to the structure of the input, for example a table for comparison, a flow diagram for a process, an outline for a hierarchical argument
Uses the cue and summary areas of a Cornell-style page to generate questions and a summary after the lecture
Constructs a concept map in which the links between concepts are labelled
Changes format when the structure of the input changes
Justifies a format choice in terms of the content and the intended use, not personal preference alone
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner three short inputs with different structures (a comparison, a process and a classification) and ask them to choose a note format for each and justify it. Check whether each format reflects the input's structure and whether relationships between items are labelled rather than merely listed.

topics.name: Taking notes in lectures
topics.description: Take notes during live or recorded lectures that capture the lecture's structure, main points, key terms, the content the lecturer flags as important, and the sources mentioned, in real time and with minimal loss of attention to the speaker. For most students, lecture notes are the main record of oral content for revision and assignments.
masteryEvidence: Produces notes whose headings reflect the lecture's macro-structure
Records the points the lecturer flags as important and marks them visually
Leaves marked gaps for missed content and fills them after the lecture
Integrates slide content with spoken additions without copying the slides
Writes an accurate 100-word summary of the lecture from the notes alone
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a 15-minute authentic lecture and collect the learner's notes, then ask for a 100-word summary written from the notes only. Check whether the notes reflect the macro-structure and the flagged points, and whether the summary is accurate and complete; gaps in the summary usually trace to gaps in the notes.

topics.name: Making notes from reading
topics.description: Make notes from academic reading that record full source details with page or location numbers and keep three kinds of content visibly separate: direct quotation (marked as such), condensed notes in one's own words, and one's own comments, questions and evaluations. Well-made reading notes are the main practical safeguard against unintentional plagiarism and the raw material for synthesis.
masteryEvidence: Records full source details and page or location numbers for every note
Marks verbatim wording with quotation marks and a page number at the moment of copying
Writes own-words notes after reading a section with the text covered, rather than while looking at it
Distinguishes their own comments and evaluations visually from source content, for example by colour, brackets or a separate column
Organises notes from several sources by theme or question
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a two-page article extract and 20 minutes to make notes for a given essay question. Check whether source details and page numbers are recorded, whether any copied wording is marked as quotation, whether the remaining notes are in the learner's own words, and whether the learner's own comments can be told apart from the source's ideas.

topics.name: Reviewing and reworking notes
topics.description: Review and rework notes after a lecture or reading through generative activities — completing gaps, summarising, generating and answering questions, reorganising into another format and self-testing at spaced intervals — rather than rereading or recopying them. Review is what turns notes from a record into learning.
masteryEvidence: Completes and corrects lecture notes within a day or two of the lecture
Writes a short summary of each set of notes in their own words
Generates questions from notes and answers them without looking
Schedules review of notes at spaced intervals across a module
Explains why self-testing is likely to be more effective than rereading or recopying notes neatly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner how they reviewed their notes before a recent test. Then give them a set of their own notes and 10 minutes to prepare for a short quiz, and observe. Check whether they reread passively or generate and answer questions, and whether they can explain the difference in likely benefit.

topics.name: Digital and handwritten note-taking
topics.description: Choose between handwritten, typed, stylus and app-based note-taking according to the task, the content (for example equations or diagrams) and personal effectiveness, use devices in ways that avoid verbatim transcription and multitasking, and organise digital notes so they can be found and reused. The evidence on laptop versus longhand notes is mixed, so the choice should rest on how notes are taken rather than on the device alone.
masteryEvidence: Explains why the evidence on laptop versus handwritten notes is inconclusive and identifies verbatim transcription and multitasking as the main risks of typing
Takes typed notes that condense and organise rather than transcribe
Manages distraction when using a device in lectures, for example by closing other applications and notifications
Organises digital notes with consistent file names, tags or folders linked to modules and sources
Chooses handwriting or stylus input for content such as equations and diagrams where typing is inefficient
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner which method they use and why, then examine a sample of their notes. Check whether their reasoning represents the evidence accurately (not 'research proves handwriting is better'), whether typed notes are verbatim or processed, and whether files are organised so that notes from a given lecture or source can be found quickly.

topics.name: Collaborative notes
topics.description: Co-construct and share notes in study groups — agreeing a common format, dividing responsibilities, cross-checking accuracy and pooling gaps — while keeping individual processing and staying within institutional rules on collusion where notes feed into individually assessed work. Shared notes can fill individual gaps but can also spread errors and reduce the processing that taking notes provides.
masteryEvidence: Agrees a shared format and a division of responsibilities for group notes
Checks and corrects peers' notes against the source
Adds their own processing (summaries, questions) instead of relying solely on shared notes
Distinguishes acceptable sharing of notes from collusion on assessed work under their institution's rules
Tracks sources and contributors in shared notes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a small group a shared document and a lecture recording and ask them to produce shared notes in 30 minutes. Review the notes and the document history: check the division of labour, evidence of cross-checking, consistency of format, and whether each member can explain the content without the notes.

topics.name: Intelligibility, comprehensibility and accent
topics.description: Distinguish intelligibility (how much of a speaker's message a listener actually understands), comprehensibility (how easy the listener finds it to understand) and accentedness (how different the speech sounds from the listener's reference variety), and use the finding that these are partly independent to set pronunciation goals around being understood rather than around imitating a particular reference accent. Intelligibility depends on listeners as well as speakers, and accent is part of a speaker's identity.
masteryEvidence: Explains the difference between intelligibility, comprehensibility and accentedness with examples
Explains why a noticeable accent does not by itself make speech hard to understand
Identifies, from listener feedback or transcription, which features of their own speech most affect understanding
Sets pronunciation goals in terms of being understood by their likely academic audiences rather than imitating a reference accent
Recognises that listener familiarity and expectations affect how well speech is understood
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to record a 1-minute explanation of a concept from their field, then ask two listeners from different language backgrounds to transcribe a section and rate how easy it was to understand. Discuss the results with the learner: check whether they can separate problems that affected understanding from features that were simply accented, and whether the goals they then set follow from that distinction.

topics.name: Word stress in academic vocabulary
topics.description: Place primary stress correctly on multi-syllable academic and technical words, including the shifts that occur across word families (ANalyse, aNALysis, anaLYtical) and the regularities associated with suffixes such as -ic, -ion, -ity and -ical, and reduce unstressed vowels appropriately. Misplaced word stress can cause listeners to misidentify words even when individual sounds are accurate.
masteryEvidence: Places stress correctly on high-frequency academic words, including derived forms in which stress shifts
Predicts stress placement for unfamiliar words with stress-attracting suffixes (-ic, -ion, -ity, -ical) and checks the prediction
Verifies stress on new vocabulary using a dictionary's stress marking or audio
Reduces unstressed vowels in multi-syllable words where appropriate, for example the first vowel of 'analysis'
Uses key academic terms in a short presentation in a way listeners recognise without difficulty
Stresses the first element of noun + noun compounds (CASE study, DATA set, CONTROL group) and the head of adjective + noun phrases (statistical SIGnificance) in technical vocabulary
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner 15 academic words including family members (economy, economic, economics; photograph, photography, photographic) and ask them to read each aloud and then use three in sentences. Check stress placement, especially in derived forms with shifted stress, and whether unstressed vowels are reduced; ask the learner to explain any pattern they used to decide.

topics.name: Thought groups and pausing
topics.description: Divide speech into thought groups — short, meaningful units usually corresponding to grammatical phrases or clauses — with pauses at group boundaries rather than within them and one main prominence in each group. Thought groups help listeners parse speech and give speakers natural planning points; pauses inside phrases make speech harder to follow.
masteryEvidence: Divides a written paragraph into thought groups at grammatical boundaries before reading it aloud
Pauses at thought-group boundaries rather than within noun phrases or between a verb and its object
Keeps long academic noun phrases together as single or linked groups
Uses longer pauses before new sections or key points
Reads aloud quotations, definitions and data in thought groups rather than word by word
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read aloud a 100-word academic paragraph after 2 minutes' preparation, and separately to speak for one minute about their subject. Check where pauses fall: at grammatical boundaries or inside phrases, and whether long noun phrases are broken into single words. Compare reading with spontaneous speech.

topics.name: Sentence stress and prominence
topics.description: Place prominence (nuclear or focal stress) on the word that carries new or contrastive information in each thought group, and de-accent information that is already given, so that listeners can identify what is important and what is being contrasted. Misplaced or absent prominence can lead listeners to misunderstand the point and to recall less of an explanation.
masteryEvidence: Places prominence on new information and moves it when that information becomes given
Uses contrastive prominence to mark a contrast (not the input but the OUTput)
De-accents repeated words in a follow-up utterance
Identifies prominent words in a recording of academic speech and explains why they are prominent
Uses prominence to make key points salient in a short presentation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short presentation extract in which new, given and contrastive information is clear, and ask them to read it aloud after 2 minutes' preparation. Check whether prominence falls on new or contrastive items and whether repeated items are de-accented; then ask the learner to explain their choices for two thought groups.

topics.name: Intonation for discourse functions
topics.description: Use pitch movement for discourse purposes in academic speaking: falling tones to present new information and close points, rising or fall-rise tones to refer to shared information, signal continuation or invite response, and pitch range and key to mark new topics and contrasts. Tone choice helps listeners follow organisation and affects how interactive and approachable a speaker sounds.
masteryEvidence: Uses falling tones on new information and on the final item of a list
Uses rising or fall-rise tones on information presented as shared or as a lead-in to a main point
Raises pitch at the start of a new section and lowers it to close a section
Distinguishes through intonation a question inviting audience response from a rhetorical question
Identifies tone choices in a recording of a lecturer and relates them to their discourse function
topics.assessmentPrompt: Record the learner giving a 2-minute explanation that includes a list, a reference back to earlier content and a section transition. Check whether new and shared information are differentiated by tone, whether the list is intoned as continuing and then complete, and whether the topic shift is marked by a pitch reset.

topics.name: Prioritised segmental features
topics.description: Identify and work on the consonant and vowel features in one's own speech that most affect intelligibility — typically contrasts with high functional load, word-final consonants and clusters that carry grammatical meaning, and vowel length or quality contrasts — rather than trying to perfect every sound. Priorities are individual: they depend on the speaker's other languages, on the listeners and on which features actually cause misunderstanding.
masteryEvidence: Identifies, from listener transcription or teacher feedback, the two or three segmental features of their own speech that most often cause misunderstanding
Distinguishes high-functional-load contrasts that need attention from lower-priority features such as the /θ/–/f/ contrast
Produces word-final consonants and clusters that carry grammatical meaning (past tense, plural) audibly in connected speech
Monitors and self-corrects a chosen segmental target in spontaneous speech
Explains why their priorities differ from those of a classmate with different language background
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to read a short paragraph and talk for a minute about their studies; ask a listener unfamiliar with the learner's first language to transcribe both. Identify words misunderstood because of segmental features. Check whether the learner can then name their priority features, and whether these are high-functional-load contrasts or grammatically meaningful endings rather than low-impact sounds.

topics.name: Connected speech in production
topics.description: Use linking within thought groups, weak forms of function words where they are unstressed, and natural reductions so that speech flows and stressed information stands out, while keeping content words and key terms clear. Moderate use of connected speech supports fluent delivery; how far full reduction helps intelligibility, particularly in lingua franca settings, is contested.
masteryEvidence: Links words within thought groups (consonant to vowel, vowel to vowel) without inserting extra pauses or vowels
Uses weak forms of frequent function words (of, to, for, and, can) in unstressed positions
Keeps content words and key terms fully articulated while reducing function words
Uses strong forms where function words are stressed or occur at the end of a phrase
Delivers frequent presentation phrases (what I'd like to do is…) as fluent units
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to deliver the opening 30 seconds of a presentation twice, once reading from a script and once from brief notes. Check for linking within thought groups and weak forms of function words, and whether any reduction blurs content words. Note whether careful articulation of every word produces a staccato rhythm that obscures which words are important.

topics.name: Pronouncing technical terms and names
topics.description: Find, check and practise the pronunciation of discipline-specific terms, proper names (theorists, places, organisations) and acronyms before using them in speech, recognising when an abbreviation is said as a word (UNESCO) or as letters (DNA) and that disciplinary communities may have their own conventions. Because key terms recur throughout an explanation, a mispronounced term can disrupt understanding of the whole.
masteryEvidence: Checks the pronunciation of new technical terms using dictionary audio, specialist glossaries or recordings of lectures and talks
Pronounces key terms in their field with the stress patterns listeners in the field expect
Distinguishes acronyms said as words from initialisms said as letters, following the conventions of their field
Checks the pronunciation of names of key authors and theorists, and accepts variation where it exists
Maintains a personal list of terms with pronunciation notes, including stress marking
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to list ten key terms and names they will use in a forthcoming presentation and to say each one aloud. Check stress placement and the treatment of acronyms, then ask how they checked each item. Look for a reliable checking method rather than pronunciation guessed from spelling.

topics.name: Self-repair and reformulation
topics.description: Notice when one's own speech has gone wrong or a listener has not understood, and repair efficiently: correcting errors that affect meaning, reformulating, and using compensatory strategies such as paraphrase, description or approximation when a word is unavailable. Effective repair keeps communication going without excessive self-correction of minor errors.
masteryEvidence: Self-corrects errors that affect meaning, such as a wrong technical term or a reversed relationship, promptly and briefly
Paraphrases or describes a concept when the target word is unavailable (it's a kind of… that…)
Recognises signs that a listener has not understood and reformulates
Signals a repair with a reformulation marker (in other words, what I mean is)
Lets minor errors that do not affect meaning pass rather than repeatedly restarting
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a short explanation task, ask the learner to explain a concept from their field without using its key term, and at one point signal that you have not understood. Check whether they paraphrase effectively, notice and respond to your signal by reformulating, and limit self-correction to errors that matter for meaning.

topics.name: Developing speech fluency
topics.description: Develop speech that flows at a rate appropriate to the audience, with pauses mainly at natural boundaries, few long hesitations inside clauses and efficient recovery, through planning, formulaic language and repeated practice. Fluency here concerns the listener's experience of smooth delivery and the speaker's processing efficiency, not speed for its own sake.
masteryEvidence: Delivers a prepared 3-minute explanation with pauses mainly at clause and thought-group boundaries
Uses pre-planned formulaic sequences (signposting, hedging and stance phrases) to reduce hesitation
Shows improved fluency across repeated performances of a task, for example in a 4/3/2 cycle
Uses pre-task planning time to plan content and key language rather than a full script
Maintains reasonable fluency when answering an unprepared question on familiar content
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to talk for 2 minutes on a familiar topic from their field, then give 5 minutes' planning time and ask them to repeat it. Note the number and location of long pauses (inside clauses or at boundaries), filled pauses and restarts. Check whether planning and repetition improve flow and whether pauses move to boundaries.

topics.name: Saying numbers, formulae and symbols aloud
topics.description: Say numbers and quantities, formulae, units, dates and symbols aloud accurately and intelligibly — large numbers and decimals, fractions and percentages, ranges and approximations, equations and units — following the conventions of one's discipline, and use the final syllable and stress to keep confusable numbers apart (thirTEEN versus THIRty). Errors with numbers in presentations and seminars can mislead listeners about findings.
masteryEvidence: Reads aloud large numbers, decimals and percentages correctly (for example 3.05 million, 0.025, 12.5%)

Distinguishes -teen and -ty numbers mainly through the final syllable (/tiːn/ versus /ti/), knowing that -teen stress shifts forward before a stressed noun (FOURteen STUdents), and confirms figures when misunderstanding is likely
Reads simple equations and formulae aloud using conventional wording (x squared, the square root of, is proportional to)
Says units and symbols in the conventional spoken form of their field and variety (kilometres per hour; p less than 0.05 said as nought point nought five or zero point zero five)
Says years, decades and ranges correctly (the 1990s, from 2010 to 2015)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a slide containing a short table of results, a formula and a date range, with 1 minute to prepare a 30-second spoken summary. Check the accuracy of number reading, the -teen/-ty distinction, the wording of the formula and units, and whether a listener could write the figures down correctly from the recording.

dependencies.reason: Locating connected-speech problems as decoding failures, rather than vocabulary gaps, motivates targeted recognition practice
Reduced forms mainly affect high-frequency function words and phrases; a listener can only map a reduced form onto a word whose citation form is already known
Linking, elision and weak forms are what obscure word boundaries, so segmentation practice presupposes recognising these processes
Using strong syllables as onset cues depends on knowing that stress placement is part of a word's stored form and that many academic words begin with an unstressed syllable
Coping with fast speech depends on segmenting and recognising words quickly enough to keep up; rate problems are largely decoding problems under time pressure
Compensatory responses to fast speech (moving on past gaps, waiting for restatement) are monitoring and problem-solving strategies
Adapting to an unfamiliar accent means remapping the phonetic cues used for segmentation and word recognition, which presupposes reasonably robust decoding of at least one variety
Understanding English as a lingua franca frames accent adaptation as normal shared work between speakers and listeners rather than as coping with deviant speech
Monitoring and diagnosing listening requires knowing what processes can fail and that different failures call for different responses
Metacognitive listening applies general person, task and strategy knowledge to the specific demands of real-time listening
Previewing slides, outlines and set readings uses the same surveying skills taught for written texts
Lecture preparation works by activating and building schemata, so learners must understand how background knowledge supports comprehension
Pre-learning a lecture's key terms draws on routines for recording and learning discipline-specific terminology
Knowledge of lecture phases is a top-down resource for meaning-building, which learners use better once they see listening as interactive
Macro-markers signal transitions between lecture phases and topics, so recognising their function presupposes a model of what is being organised
Micro-markers such as so, now and right are usually unstressed and reduced, so recognising them depends on decoding connected speech
Relevance markers are a distinct class of lecture metadiscourse that is easier to isolate once organisational markers are familiar
Recognising prosodic emphasis as a signal of importance presupposes awareness of how prominence and pausing mark focal information
Selecting central content in real time relies on the speaker's own signals of what matters
Building a representation of an extended argument requires decoding fluent enough at natural rates to leave attention for meaning-building
The distinction between central claims and elaboration is usually first taught in reading, where the text can be revisited
Following extended academic speech depends on adequate lexical coverage, of which general academic vocabulary is a large component
Recognising a departure from the main thread presupposes a representation of what the main thread is
Inferring a speaker's evaluation of a position requires first following the positions and claims being evaluated
Recognising stance in lectures draws on knowledge of the lexical and phrasal resources speakers use to express and mitigate stance
Scepticism, irony and degrees of commitment are often carried by tone and pitch range rather than by words alone
Tracking participants' positions and how contributions respond to one another requires inferring each speaker's stance
Seminar groups in international universities bring together many accents, often in quick succession
Understanding seminars as co-constructed discussion explains why contributions build on and challenge each other, which is what listeners must track
Deciding whether to attend to the slide or the speaker at a given moment depends on judging where the central content is
Following a spoken explanation of a chart requires reading axes, scales and features of the visual being discussed
Reviewing slides in advance frees attention during the lecture for the spoken channel
Targeted replay depends on monitoring during the live lecture and evaluating afterwards what was missed and why
Using recordings well means applying retrieval and spacing rather than low-utility passive review
Recordings are most useful for repairing and completing notes taken during the live lecture
Briefings and announcements are built on institutional terms (module, submission, extension, assessment brief) that must be understood to act on them
Assignment briefings restate task demands using command words whose meaning determines what students must do
Briefings and announcements are usually unscripted and delivered in reduced connected speech, sometimes over poor audio
Extracting relevant content from long, loosely structured recordings depends on identifying main points in extended speech
Recorded talks and podcasts expose listeners to a wider range of speakers and accents than their own lecturers
Treating a podcast or talk as an academic source requires the same judgements of authority, currency and evidence as written sources
Knowing that notes must later serve as a usable record, and that condensing promotes processing, gives learners the criteria for what to select
Selecting what to note depends on distinguishing central claims from elaboration and examples, a skill usually established first in reading
Shorthand is only useful if notes remain decodable when reviewed, which follows from the external-storage function
Conventional academic abbreviations (e.g., i.e., cf.) form part of the shorthand repertoire and must be used with their correct meanings
Symbols for cause, contrast and consequence encode the logical relations that linking adverbials express, so learners need those relations first
A format organises selected content; without selection, any format becomes transcription in a different layout
Matching format to content requires recognising patterns such as comparison, process, problem–solution and classification
Real-time lecture notes depend on identifying main points and their support as the lecture unfolds
Lecture notes apply a chosen format under time pressure, so the format must already be familiar
Shorthand makes it possible to keep pace with speech while preserving relations between ideas
Reading notes require the same selection of main ideas and relevant detail, adjusted to purpose
Purposeful annotation is usually the first pass from which reading notes are made
Understanding why source wording, source ideas and one's own ideas must be distinguished motivates the separation that reading notes build in
Generative review of notes applies retrieval practice and spacing, and rejects low-utility rereading and highlighting
Reworking notes often means reorganising them into a different format (for example a Cornell cue column, a table or a concept map)
The device question arises mainly in real-time lecture note-taking, where typing speed invites transcription
Digital notes are only reusable if files are consistently named, organised and backed up
Shared notes require an agreed format, which presupposes knowing the options and their uses
Collaborative notes are usually built in shared documents with comments and version history
Students must know where permitted sharing of notes ends and collusion on assessed work begins
Prioritising word stress follows from knowing that stress errors affect intelligibility more than many segmental differences
Stress shift across derived forms can only be learnt once learners know the members of the word family and the suffixes that derive them
Suffix-based stress regularities (-ic, -ion, -ity) depend on recognising those suffixes
Thought groups are taught as a high-priority prosodic feature because of their effect on listeners' ability to process speech
Placing boundaries at grammatical constituents requires recognising phrases and clause elements, especially in long academic noun phrases
Prominence is assigned within a thought group, each group having one main focus, so the group must be identified first
Prominence is realised on the stressed syllable of the focal word, so word stress must be correctly placed
Prominence work makes the given–new distinction audible; the written-discourse treatment can follow or run in parallel
Tone choices are realised from the prominent (tonic) syllable, so prominence placement must already be controlled
Understanding that speech signals organisation through prosody where writing uses punctuation and layout motivates intonation work in academic speaking
Choosing which sounds to work on depends on the intelligibility principle and on evidence of what listeners actually misunderstand
Learners usually need to recognise weak forms and linking in others' speech before they can use them appropriately
Reduction applies to unstressed, non-prominent words, so learners need control of what is prominent before reducing what is not
Pronouncing technical terms correctly is largely a matter of placing stress correctly on long, often derived words
Learners must know which terms are central in their field, and what they mean, before practising them for speech
Checking pronunciation relies on reading dictionary stress marks and transcriptions or using audio
Deciding which errors need repair depends on judging what affects the listener's understanding
Paraphrasing an unavailable term typically uses definition-like structures (a kind of X that…)
Reformulation markers such as in other words and that is signal a repair to the listener
Pausing at thought-group boundaries rather than inside phrases is a central feature of perceived fluency
Retrieving spoken formulas as wholes reduces the online planning load that causes hesitation
Efficient repair and compensation keep speech moving when a word or structure is not available, rather than halting it
Saying quantities aloud presupposes understanding and writing numbers, fractions, decimals and percentages accurately
Keeping -teen and -ty numbers apart, and saying long unit names intelligibly, depends on stress placement
Reading equations aloud follows the conventions for expressing variables and operations in words

guidance.summary: Field (2008) argues that the conventional comprehension approach (listen, answer questions, check answers) tests listening without teaching it, and proposes diagnosing which processes fail. Vandergrift and Goh (2012) similarly treat listening as interacting bottom-up and top-down processes managed by metacognition. For EAP learners the payoff is practical: once they can name where listening breaks down, they can choose targeted practice rather than simply 'more listening'. Keep the model light and anchored in learners' own listening data rather than presented as theory.

activities.title: Transcribe, then explain
learnerActions: Listen twice to a 20–30-second unscripted extract and write down exactly what the speaker said, leaving gaps where unsure
Compare the transcript with the original and mark each mismatch
Sort each mismatch: a known word not recognised, an unknown word, or words heard but the meaning missed
Discuss which category dominated and what that implies for practice
activities.intendedInsight: Many failures happen at word recognition even when the vocabulary is known, and comprehension questions alone hide this.
activities.rationale: Field's process approach uses short transcription and error analysis to expose decoding breakdowns that answer-checking conceals; Goh's diary study found learners frequently reported not recognising words they knew.

activities.title: Listening problem log
learnerActions: After each lecture or practice task, note one moment where understanding broke down and what seemed to happen
Classify each entry as a decoding or a meaning-building problem using a short checklist
Review the log fortnightly with a peer and choose one targeted practice activity
activities.intendedInsight: Listening problems are specific and patterned, so practice can be chosen rather than left to general exposure.
activities.rationale: Vandergrift and Goh's metacognitive approach uses reflection on listening problems to build person and task knowledge; a log makes that reflection routine.

difficulties.pattern: 'My only problem is vocabulary — if I knew more words I would understand.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners can read the transcript of an extract fluently but could not follow it aurally, yet attribute every failure to unknown words.
difficulties.response: Show the transcript after listening and ask learners to underline words they knew but did not catch; the gap between known and recognised words makes the decoding problem visible. Do not dismiss vocabulary size, which does constrain listening, but separate it from speed and accuracy of recognition.

difficulties.pattern: Learners build a plausible interpretation from a few recognised words and topic expectations, and are confident in it even when it is wrong.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that are coherent but contradict the extract, often reflecting what the learner expected the speaker to say.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to verify each prediction against specific words heard on a second listening, and praise checking rather than fluent guessing. Do not teach 'guess from context' as a stand-alone remedy for weak decoders; Field cautions that compensatory strategies cannot substitute for accurate decoding.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe the last time they failed to understand part of a lecture and why. Then play a 20-second extract and ask them to point to where they lost track and whether they heard the words at that point.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Locates specific moments, distinguishes not catching words from not understanding the point, and suggests different remedies for each.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies breakdown points but attributes all of them to vocabulary or speed without distinguishing processes.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Reports global failure ('it was too fast', 'I understood nothing') and cannot locate or characterise breakdowns.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, present the model through concrete examples and learners' own transcripts rather than terminology. On pre-sessional courses it can frame the whole listening syllabus and justify the balance of short decoding work and extended lecture listening. In-sessionally it is most useful in one-to-one or small-group diagnosis with students who report persistent difficulty in lectures. Persistent difficulty that does not respond to decoding practice may reflect a hearing or auditory processing difference rather than a language problem; refer the student to disability or learning support services and offer captions or transcripts in the meantime.

guidance.summary: Learners often know a word in writing but fail to recognise its reduced spoken form; Goh (2000) found that not recognising known words was among the problems learners most often reported. Field (2008) recommends short, intensive decoding exercises with authentic or semi-scripted speech, attending to the forms words take in context rather than in isolation, and Rost (2011) describes reduction, assimilation and elision as regular processes that can be taught. Prioritise recognition before production, focus on the high-frequency function words and phrases where most reduction occurs, and keep extracts short enough for close attention.

activities.title: Gapped transcription of function words
learnerActions: Listen to a 10–15-second lecture extract with a transcript from which the function words have been removed
Fill each gap, replaying as needed
Compare with the full transcript and note which weak forms were missed
Repeat with a new extract that features the same forms
activities.intendedInsight: The words that are hardest to hear are often the shortest and most familiar.
activities.rationale: Field's process approach targets the specific forms that cause recognition failure; gapping function words directs attention to weak forms rather than to content words, which learners already prioritise.

activities.title: Citation form versus connected form
learnerActions: Hear a phrase spoken word by word and then in natural connected speech
Write down what changed: sounds lost, merged or linked
Find two further examples of the same pattern in a lecture recording
activities.intendedInsight: Connected-speech changes are systematic, so a small number of patterns explains many recognition problems.
activities.rationale: Rost (2011) presents reduction, assimilation and elision as regular features of spoken English; contrasting the two forms makes the regularities noticeable.

difficulties.pattern: 'Lecturers swallow their words — they don't speak clearly.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners attribute recognition failure to the speaker and expect every word to be fully articulated, as in scripted course-book audio.
difficulties.response: Explain that reduction is normal in fluent speech in every language, including learners' own, and that unstressed words carry little acoustic information because listeners are expected to predict them. Use L1 examples where the group can supply them. Do not present asking lecturers to 'speak clearly' as the main solution.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language gives syllables similar prominence and reduces vowels little expect every syllable to be equally clear and do not register reduced vowels.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcriptions omit or misidentify unstressed function words, and learners insert full vowels when repeating reduced phrases.
difficulties.response: Contrast stressed and unstressed syllables explicitly, using the schwa as a focal point, and practise recognising strings containing several weak forms. Production work can follow, but prioritise recognition first.

difficulties.pattern: Learners have practised mainly with scripted, slowly delivered recordings, so their first authentic lectures feel unintelligible.
difficulties.revealedBy: A large gap between scores on course-book listening and comprehension of authentic lecture extracts.
difficulties.response: Introduce short authentic or semi-scripted extracts early, with transcripts, so that exposure to connected speech is gradual but real.

diagnostic.task: Play a 15-second lecture extract twice and ask for a word-for-word transcription.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Content and function words are largely restored, including weak forms and reduced sequences; errors are minor and do not affect parsing.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Content words are mostly captured but many function words are missing or wrong, and some reduced sequences are misanalysed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Only isolated content words are captured; the transcript cannot be parsed as sentences.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and early pre-sessional level, short intensive decoding work should feature in most listening lessons. Later it is best used diagnostically: when in-sessional students report not being able to follow a particular lecturer, close transcription of a short extract often shows reduction rather than vocabulary to be the barrier.

guidance.summary: Listeners to English exploit the tendency for content words to begin with a strong syllable (one with a full, unreduced vowel) when hypothesising where words start; Field (2003, 2008) reviews this research and proposes explicit segmentation training for L2 listeners, whose first languages may use different boundary cues. Teaching should combine noticing of strong syllables with lexical and grammatical checking, because a segmentation hypothesis is confirmed or revised as more of the utterance arrives. Short extracts, replay and comparison with transcripts suit this kind of close work.

activities.title: Find the strong syllables first
learnerActions: Listen to a short sentence and mark each strong (clearly pronounced, often stressed) syllable on a line
Predict where content words begin, using the strong syllables
Replay and write the full sentence, checking the predictions
activities.intendedInsight: Strong syllables are useful landmarks for finding content words, although not infallible ones.
activities.rationale: Field (2003) proposes training L2 listeners to use strong syllables as segmentation cues, as listeners to English do.

activities.title: Mishearing repair
learnerActions: Read pairs of plausible mishearings collected from learner transcripts
Listen to the original and decide which version was said
Explain which cue (stress, linking, grammar, context) resolves the ambiguity
activities.intendedInsight: Segmentation is a hypothesis to be checked against grammar and context, not a one-off decision.
activities.rationale: Field (2008) treats word recognition as tentative and revised as listening proceeds; repairing plausible errors rehearses this checking.

difficulties.pattern: Learners may transfer the segmentation routines of their first language (for example syllable-based segmentation in French or mora-based segmentation in Japanese) or expect stress at a fixed position in the word, so English strong syllables are not used, or are misused, as onset cues. The effect is not uniform: listeners whose first language has fixed initial stress may already treat a stressed onset as a likely word boundary.
difficulties.revealedBy: Boundary errors cluster around words that begin with an unstressed syllable (economy, consider, analysis), which are attached to or split from neighbouring words.
difficulties.response: Teach explicitly that weak-initial words are the main exception to the strong-onset tendency and therefore the main source of boundary errors; practise prefix-initial academic words (con-, de-, re-) in context, linked to word-stress work. Diagnose from transcripts rather than assuming a problem from the learner's first language.

difficulties.pattern: Learners commit to the first segmentation they make and interpret the rest of the sentence to fit it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcripts with an early mis-segmentation followed by a forced or ungrammatical reading of the rest of the sentence.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to flag uncertain words during a first listening and revisit them at the end of the sentence; model revision aloud. Accept tentative transcriptions with marked alternatives rather than penalising them.
