diagnostic.task: Play a 10-second extract that includes a word beginning with a weak syllable and a linked sequence; ask for a transcription and then ask the learner to explain any revisions they made.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Places boundaries correctly, or corrects an initial error on replay and gives a reason (stress, grammar, context).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Places most boundaries correctly but does not notice errors around weak-initial words.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes non-words or merges and splits words without noticing that the result is ungrammatical.

guidance.contextNotes: Most important at foundation and pre-sessional level, particularly for learners who have learnt English mainly through reading. In-sessionally, segmentation problems resurface with new technical vocabulary, where learners lack the lexical knowledge to check a hypothesis; pairing listening with pre-taught terminology may help.
reviewNotes: Review response (R2-06): terminology now distinguishes strong (full-vowel) syllables from stressed syllables, and the L1 mechanism is restated as transfer of segmentation routines. The primary sources the reviewer suggested (Cutler & Carter, 1987; Cutler, 2012) are not in the closed bibliography; the claim is cited through Field (2003), which reviews that research, and they could be added if the bibliography is extended.

guidance.summary: Speed is the problem learners most often name (Graham, 2006), and slower delivery can improve comprehension (Griffiths, 1992). Slowed input is a scaffold rather than a solution, however: Field (2008) attributes much of the sense of speed to decoding that is not yet automatic, so the longer-term remedy is extensive and repeated listening that builds fast word recognition. In the short term, teach learners to keep pace by letting go of missed words and using the restatement and redundancy typical of lecture discourse.

activities.title: Graduated speed replay
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract at reduced speed with a transcript
Listen again at reduced speed without the transcript
Listen at natural speed and summarise
Record which sections still caused problems and why
activities.intendedInsight: Recognition at natural speed tends to improve with repeated exposure to the same speaker and material.
activities.rationale: Griffiths (1992) found slower rates aided comprehension; here rate reduction is used as a scaffold that is withdrawn within the task, moving learners towards natural rates rather than dependence on slow input.

activities.title: Keep going
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section and tick a box each time a word or phrase is lost, but keep listening
After listening, note what was later recovered through restatement, examples or summary
Compare with a partner which missed points were recovered and how
activities.intendedInsight: Lectures repeat and reformulate key content, so missing a word is rarely fatal if attention stays on the stream.
activities.rationale: Goh (2000) found that learners lose subsequent input while dwelling on an earlier problem; practising the decision to move on targets that pattern.

difficulties.pattern: 'Everyone speaks too fast — I need them to slow down.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners rate all authentic material as too fast regardless of actual rate, report low confidence and avoid authentic listening.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge the experience, then make progress visible by tracking improvement on the same speaker across repeated listenings; Graham (2006) found learners tend to attribute listening failure to low ability, which undermines persistence. Do not rely only on slowed or scripted material, which delays adaptation to real lectures.

difficulties.pattern: Learners stop to translate or work out a missed word and lose the next segment.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries capture the first part of an extract well and little or nothing after a difficult word.
difficulties.response: Practise continuing past gaps and show that later restatement often resolves them. Avoid pausing recordings after every sentence for comprehension checks, which reinforces word-by-word processing.

difficulties.pattern: Recognition of frequent words is not yet automatic, so even moderate rates overload the learner.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcriptions show missing frequent words even in slower speech.
difficulties.response: Increase the volume of comprehensible listening (graded podcasts, repeated listening to the same recording) and continue decoding work. Strategy instruction alone will not solve this.

diagnostic.task: Play two comparable 60-second extracts by the same speaker, one at 0.8 and one at natural speed, and ask for the key points after each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Captures the main points at natural speed, with only minor additional detail at reduced speed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures main points only at reduced speed but continues to follow the thread at natural speed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Loses the thread at natural speed after the first difficulty and recovers little even at reduced speed.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, slowed or semi-scripted material can bridge to authentic rates but should not replace them. Pre-sessional courses should include unscripted lecture extracts from the outset. In-sessional students facing a fast lecturer benefit most from repeated listening to recordings of that lecturer, which builds speaker-specific familiarity.
reviewNotes: Lecture speech rates vary widely by speaker, discipline and phase; this record deliberately avoids giving a words-per-minute threshold.

guidance.summary: Accent familiarity affects listening: Major et al. (2002) found that listening test scores could be lower when lectures were delivered by speakers the study classed as non-native, and a shared first language did not consistently help. Perceptual research indicates that listeners adapt to an unfamiliar accent with exposure, and that exposure to several speakers of an accent supports generalisation to new speakers (Bradlow & Bent, 2008). Jenkins (2014) argues that international universities are lingua franca settings in which native-speaker accents should not be treated as the default. Teaching should broaden exposure, build adaptation, and address listener attitudes as well as perception.

activities.title: Accent exposure ladder
learnerActions: Listen two or three times each to short academic talks by several speakers who share an accent
Transcribe a short section from each and note recurring features that caused errors
Listen to a new speaker with the same accent and compare accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Adaptation generalises better when exposure includes several speakers rather than one.
activities.rationale: Bradlow and Bent (2008) report that multi-talker exposure supported talker-independent adaptation to foreign-accented speech; the activity applies this to academic listening as a proposal, not as a tested EAP intervention.

activities.title: Whose accent counts as standard?
learnerActions: Map the accents of lecturers and classmates they will meet, for example from departmental video introductions
Discuss which they find easier and why (familiarity, rate, signposting)
Agree listening and clarification strategies that do not assume one variety is correct
activities.intendedInsight: Difficulty depends on the listener's familiarity and expectations as well as on the speaker.
activities.rationale: Jenkins (2014) documents the dominance of native-speaker norms in university language policy and argues for a lingua franca perspective; making expectations explicit addresses the attitudinal side of accent comprehension.

difficulties.pattern: 'I can only understand British (or American) English; other accents are wrong.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Strong preference for one prestige variety, reflecting materials used in previous study; dismissive comments about lecturers' or peers' accents.
difficulties.response: Broaden exposure deliberately and discuss the international make-up of staff and students. Rubin (1992) found that listeners' expectations about a speaker affected their comprehension of identical speech, which helps frame accent comprehension as partly the listener's responsibility.

difficulties.pattern: Learners give up on an unfamiliar speaker within the first minute.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension of the opening of a talk is low and does not improve, because attention has been withdrawn.
difficulties.response: Show improvement curves from repeated exposure and set short, achievable goals for new speakers. Avoid restricting early-level learners to 'easy' accents, which delays adaptation.

difficulties.pattern: Words are misrecognised when a speaker places lexical stress differently from the pattern the learner expects.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcription errors cluster on multi-syllable words with shifted stress.
difficulties.response: Use transcription comparison to identify the feature, then practise with that speaker. Field (2005) found that misplaced stress disrupted recognition for both the native and the non-native listeners in his study, so this is a normal listener difficulty rather than a learner deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Listening materials and tests draw almost entirely on a narrow set of prestige accents, so learners first meet the range of accents used at their university in their lectures.
difficulties.revealedBy: Course audio and practice tests feature one or two varieties; learners who score well on them report being unable to follow particular lecturers or peers.
difficulties.response: Course teams should audit listening materials for the range of accents they include and add recordings of lecturers and students from the target institution, with permission. Learners can be shown how to find varied recordings for independent listening.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to listen to a 90-second extract by a speaker whose accent they find difficult and summarise it, then listen to a further 2 minutes by the same speaker and summarise a new section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The second summary is markedly more accurate, and the learner can name what caused the initial difficulty.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some improvement, but the learner cannot identify the cause of difficulty.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No improvement; the learner disengages or dismisses the accent as 'bad English'.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional programmes often rely on a narrow range of audio sources; widen these early. In-sessionally, the key accents are those of the student's own lecturers and peers, and lecture recordings allow targeted exposure. For PGR students, conferences and research seminars bring the widest range of accents, often with less signposting.
reviewNotes: Review response (R5-18): topic text now avoids the native/non-native binary except when reporting the categories used by Major et al. (2002) and Field (2005).

guidance.summary: Vandergrift and Goh (2012) propose a metacognitive pedagogical sequence — planning and predicting, first verification, second verification, final verification and reflection — that embeds strategy use in repeated listening to the same text. Vandergrift and Tafaghodtari (2010) reported that learners taught in this way outperformed a comparison group, with less skilled listeners gaining most. Field (2008) cautions that strategies compensate for decoding gaps rather than remove them, so metacognitive work should run alongside decoding practice rather than replace it.

activities.title: Metacognitive listening cycle
learnerActions: Predict the content and some vocabulary of a lecture extract from its title and first slide
Listen and check predictions, noting difficulties
Compare with a partner and listen again for unresolved points
Listen once more with a transcript for final verification
Write a short reflection on what helped and what to try next time
activities.intendedInsight: Listening can be managed rather than simply endured.
activities.rationale: Follows the pedagogical sequence described by Vandergrift and Goh (2012) and examined empirically by Vandergrift and Tafaghodtari (2010).

activities.title: Listening diary
learnerActions: Record each week what they listened to, what was difficult and what they tried
Rate their confidence for each listening
Review entries monthly to identify recurring patterns and set a new goal
activities.intendedInsight: Knowledge of oneself as a listener is built through reflection over time.
activities.rationale: Goh (2000) used learner diaries to reveal listening problems; reflection develops the person, task and strategy knowledge that Flavell (1979) identifies as metacognitive knowledge.

difficulties.pattern: Learners equate 'strategy' with guessing and rely on it in place of listening closely.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident but inaccurate summaries; little change between first and second listening.
difficulties.response: Emphasise the verification stages of the cycle and make learners point to the words that support each inference. Revisit the distinction between decoding and meaning-building.

difficulties.pattern: Learners treat reflection as a task done for the teacher and write generic entries.
difficulties.revealedBy: Log entries such as 'it was difficult' or 'I need more practice' with no specific moment or action.
difficulties.response: Model specific entries, keep logs short, and link each reflection to a concrete practice choice the learner then carries out.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What do you do when you lose track during a lecture?' Then ask about the last time it happened.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes specific monitoring and repair actions linked to the type of problem, and some evaluation of whether they worked.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions general strategies ('I try to guess') without linking them to problem types or evaluating them.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Says they stop listening, or has no strategies beyond asking a friend later.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level the cycle can be run fully with teacher guidance on short texts. On pre-sessional courses it should become a routine learners can run independently with recordings. In-sessionally, the reflective log is the most portable element and works well in self-access or tutorial settings.

guidance.summary: The planning stage of Vandergrift and Goh's (2012) metacognitive cycle — setting goals and predicting content and vocabulary — is the classroom counterpart of lecture preparation. Prior knowledge supports meaning-building, but Field (2008) cautions that strong expectations can lead listeners to hear what they predicted, so predictions must be checked rather than trusted. Slides and readings posted in advance make preparation feasible for many lectures; the teaching task is to turn them into a short, sustainable routine that includes how key terms sound.

activities.title: Twenty-minute preparation routine
learnerActions: Skim the slides and note the likely sections
List up to ten key terms and check their meaning and pronunciation
Write three questions the lecture is likely to answer
After the lecture, tick the questions answered and note anything unexpected
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation makes a lecture more predictable, but predictions must be checked against what is said.
activities.rationale: Applies the planning and verification stages of Vandergrift and Goh's (2012) pedagogical cycle to lecture listening.

activities.title: Prediction versus delivery
learnerActions: Predict the content of a lecture section from its slide
Listen and note where the lecture went beyond or departed from the slide
Discuss what would have been missed by relying on the slides alone
activities.intendedInsight: Slides outline a lecture; they do not contain it.
activities.rationale: Field (2008) notes that top-down expectation can override what is actually said; contrasting prediction with input trains checking.

difficulties.pattern: 'I don't have time to prepare for every lecture.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Preparation is attempted in full for a week or two and then abandoned.
difficulties.response: Teach a minimal 10-minute version (structure and key terms only) for heavy weeks, and a fuller version for the most difficult modules.

difficulties.pattern: Learners pre-learn the spelling and meaning of key terms but not their pronunciation, so do not recognise them when spoken.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners know a term in writing but report never hearing it in the lecture where it was used repeatedly.
difficulties.response: Build pronunciation checking (dictionary audio, earlier lecture recordings) into term preparation, with stress marked on the term list.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read the slides thoroughly beforehand and then stop listening attentively during the lecture.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lecture notes simply reproduce slide text.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to annotate slides during the lecture only with what is said and not shown, and review those annotations afterwards.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner what they did before their last lecture, then give them a slide deck and 10 minutes to prepare while you observe.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Works systematically: identifies structure, lists terms with pronunciation, writes predictions, and explains how they will use them during the lecture.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Reads the slides and checks the meaning of some vocabulary, without structure or pronunciation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does no preparation, or reads the slides without any specific focus.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, preparation can be scaffolded with teacher-provided term lists and prediction questions. Pre-sessional courses should build independence. In-sessionally, students' real module materials make the routine immediately useful, and PGT students with heavy reading loads need efficient, prioritised preparation.

guidance.summary: Young (1994) identified recurring phases in university lectures — discourse structuring, conclusion and evaluation, alongside content, exemplification and interaction — and showed that they interweave rather than occurring in a fixed order, so a lecturer may return to structuring talk many times. Teaching these phases gives learners a top-down frame for meaning-building, but the frame should be presented as a set of expectations, not a template: lectures vary by discipline and lecturer, and interactive formats have become more common (Lynch, 2011).

activities.title: Phase mapping
learnerActions: Listen to a 10-minute lecture extract
Mark each phase on a timeline using colour codes (structuring, content, example, evaluation, interaction)
Compare timelines in groups and replay disputed sections
Identify which phases contained the information they would note
activities.intendedInsight: Lectures repeatedly signal their own structure, and those signals are chances to reorient.
activities.rationale: Applies Young's (1994) phase model; comparing maps shows how phases interleave.

activities.title: Two lecture styles
learnerActions: Watch extracts from a closely scripted lecture and an interactive one on related content
Note where structure is signalled and where it must be inferred
Discuss what each style demands of the listener
activities.intendedInsight: How explicitly structure is signalled varies, so listeners sometimes have to build the structure themselves.
activities.rationale: Lynch (2011) reviews changes in lecture formats towards greater interactivity; contrasting styles prepares learners for variation rather than a single model.

difficulties.pattern: 'The introduction is just the lecturer talking; the real lecture starts later.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners miss or do not note the preview and later cannot see how sections relate.
difficulties.response: Show how the preview predicts the lecture's sections, use it to set up a note frame, and return to it at the end of the lecture.

difficulties.pattern: Learners expect lectures to follow the tidy linear structure of course-book recordings and are disoriented by recursion, asides and interaction.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion when a lecturer returns to an earlier point or opens questions mid-lecture.
difficulties.response: Use authentic lectures early and treat phase switching as normal; Young's (1994) finding that phases interweave is a useful framing to share with learners.

diagnostic.task: Play the first 3 minutes of a lecture and ask the learner to predict the sections of the rest; then play two later 1-minute segments and ask which section and which phase each belongs to.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Predicts sections accurately from the preview, identifies phases correctly and explains the cues used.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Predicts sections but misclassifies evaluation or example phases as content.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot use the preview to predict, and experiences the lecture as undifferentiated.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from explicit phase labels applied to short, well-structured lectures on familiar topics. Pre-sessional courses should use full-length authentic lectures and link phases to note frames. In-sessionally, analysing a recording from a student's own module reveals discipline- and lecturer-specific patterns.

guidance.summary: Chaudron and Richards (1986) found that macro-markers aided recall of a lecture whereas micro-markers did not, while Flowerdew and Tauroza (1995) found that micro-markers did aid comprehension; the effect of markers is therefore not uniform and probably depends on listeners and materials. Thompson (2003) showed that lecturers signal organisation through intonation as well as words, and that listening materials tend to under-represent this. Teach a working inventory of macro-markers drawn from authentic lecture language, such as the discourse-organising bundles Biber et al. (2004) found in classroom teaching, and draw attention to prosodic boundaries.

activities.title: Marker hunt and prediction
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section and pause after each macro-marker
Predict what will come next (new topic, example, summary, return)
Continue listening to check the prediction
Add the marker to a personal list organised by function
activities.intendedInsight: Markers are cues for prediction, not just phrases to recognise.
activities.rationale: Uses macro-markers, which Chaudron and Richards (1986) found aided recall, as triggers for top-down prediction.

activities.title: Hearing structure without words
learnerActions: Listen to an extract in which a topic shift is signalled by a pause and pitch reset with little lexical signalling
Mark where they think a new section begins
Compare with a transcript and discuss which cues they used
activities.intendedInsight: Lecturers signal structure through the voice as well as through words.
activities.rationale: Thompson (2003) found intonation working alongside text-structuring metadiscourse in lectures; this targets a cue that materials under-represent.

difficulties.pattern: Learners listen for formal written connectors (firstly, in conclusion) and miss the informal markers lecturers actually use (so, right, OK, what we're going to look at now).
difficulties.revealedBy: Topic transitions marked by informal or reduced markers go unnoticed; notes run sections together.
difficulties.response: Build the marker inventory from lecture corpora and recordings rather than from written connector lists; Biber et al. (2004) show that classroom teaching uses many discourse-organising bundles that differ from written ones.

difficulties.pattern: Short micro-markers are not perceived because they are unstressed and run into the following words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transcriptions omit so, now, right, and learners do not notice the shift these words signal.
difficulties.response: Include marker-plus-clause sequences in short decoding exercises, treating recognition of markers as a decoding goal as well as a discourse one.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a transcript of a 2-minute lecture extract with the markers removed; ask them to listen, insert the markers they hear and label each one's function.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Inserts most markers, including informal ones, with correct functions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures formal macro-markers but misses or mislabels informal or reduced micro-markers.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Captures few markers and cannot identify their functions.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners need explicit inventories and recognition practice; later pre-sessional work should shift to prediction and to lecturers who signal less explicitly. In-sessionally, the focus moves to discipline- and lecturer-specific signalling habits, including transitions led by slides rather than by speech.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-18): coh.spoken-signposting has been merged into prs.signposting (production). This topic is the reception counterpart. The former soft edge from prs.signposting has been removed so that the PRS strand can make prs.signposting depend on this topic (recognition before production) without creating a cycle.

guidance.summary: Deroey and Taverniers (2012) catalogued the lexicogrammatical patterns lecturers use to mark relevance and showed that these markers both highlight content and manage what students should attend to, including what will be assessed. Because importance is also marked prosodically (Thompson, 2003), teaching should combine an inventory of verbal markers with attention to stress, pausing and repetition. Learners should practise acting on markers — starring, boxing, prioritising in review — not just recognising them.

activities.title: Relevance marker log
learnerActions: Listen to an authentic lecture and pause each time the lecturer marks something as important or unimportant
Write down the marker and the point it flags
Group the markers by form (verb, noun, adjective or adverb, reference to assessment, voice only)
Compare the flagged points with the lecture's slides and note any that appeared only in speech
activities.intendedInsight: Lecturers repeatedly tell students what matters, and the signals can be learnt.
activities.rationale: Builds on the types of lexicogrammatical relevance markers identified in lecture data by Deroey and Taverniers (2012).

activities.title: Spot the emphasis
learnerActions: Read a transcript of a lecture extract from which verbal relevance markers have been removed
Listen and mark where the speaker signals importance through voice alone
Compare with the original recording and transcript
activities.intendedInsight: Importance is signalled through the voice as well as through words.
activities.rationale: Thompson (2003) showed that intonation contributes to signalling in lectures alongside metadiscourse.

difficulties.pattern: Learners give every point equal weight and do not respond to signals of importance.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes without hierarchy; points the lecturer flagged as key are missing from recall tasks.
difficulties.response: Teach relevance markers explicitly and require visual prioritisation (stars, boxes) in notes; review notes against a list of the points the lecturer flagged.

difficulties.pattern: Learners attend mainly to lexical content and, especially when decoding load is high, do not use the speaker's voice (heavy stress, slowing, pausing, repetition) as a cue to importance.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners catch verbal relevance markers but miss points emphasised by voice alone.
difficulties.response: Contrast the same sentence delivered with and without emphatic stress and ask what changes; link to production work on prominence so that perception and production reinforce each other.

difficulties.pattern: 'If it isn't on the slides, it isn't important.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Attention drops when the lecturer moves away from slide content; points flagged orally are absent from notes.
difficulties.response: Show examples in which lecturers flag oral-only content as important or assessable, and ask learners to collect such moments from their own lectures.

diagnostic.task: After a 10-minute extract, ask: 'What three things did the lecturer most want you to remember, and how did you know?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Retrieves the flagged points and names verbal or prosodic cues for each.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Retrieves some flagged points but relies on slide content, or cannot say how importance was signalled.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists points at random or simply the first points heard, with no awareness of signalling.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need explicit teaching with clear examples. In-sessional UG and PGT students benefit from analysing their own lecturers' relevance marking, which can be idiosyncratic and is often tied to assessment.

guidance.summary: Selecting main points draws on meaning-building: listeners construct a representation of the speaker's argument and decide what is central, using discourse cues and prior knowledge (Field, 2008; Rost, 2011). It also depends on decoding fluency and vocabulary: Nation (2006) estimated that around 6,000–7,000 word families are needed for 98% coverage of spoken English, and van Zeeland and Schmitt (2013) suggest adequate listening comprehension may be possible at somewhat lower coverage, with considerable individual variation. Main-point work should therefore be paired with vocabulary development and should move from cue-supported selection towards inferring importance where cues are sparse.

activities.title: Rank and justify
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section and note up to six points
In pairs, rank the points by importance and justify the ranking with cues heard (previews, relevance markers, time spent, summaries)
Compare the ranking with the lecturer's own summary or slides
activities.intendedInsight: Importance is signalled by several converging cues that can be used deliberately.
activities.rationale: Encourages meaning-building that integrates discourse cues, as described by Field (2008).

activities.title: Claim or support?
learnerActions: Read a list of statements taken from a lecture they have just heard
Label each as main claim, example, evidence or restatement
Rebuild a hierarchy diagram of the section and check it against the recording
activities.intendedInsight: Main points and supporting material have different functions, which determines what to note and how.
activities.rationale: Making the hierarchy explicit connects listening comprehension to note-taking and summary.

difficulties.pattern: Learners treat memorable details (figures, names, vivid examples) as the main points.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries list salient details but omit the more abstract claim they supported.
difficulties.response: After each example, ask 'What was this an example of?' and practise abstracting from examples to claims. Avoid teaching 'note the numbers' as a general strategy.

difficulties.pattern: Decoding takes so much attention that little is left for following the argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners can repeat phrases verbatim but cannot say what the point was.
difficulties.response: Reduce decoding load through preparation and repeated listening, then focus a later listening on structure. Do not read this as a lack of critical or analytical ability.

difficulties.pattern: Learners expect each main point to be stated explicitly once, as in a topic sentence, and miss points developed cumulatively.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners identify explicitly announced points but not points the lecturer builds towards inductively.
difficulties.response: Use lectures with inductive structure and ask learners to formulate the point the lecturer was building towards before it is stated.

diagnostic.task: After a 5-minute extract, ask for the main point in one sentence and two supporting details.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Abstracts the main point accurately and subordinates the details correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Captures the main point only partly or confuses it with a detail; the details themselves are accurate.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists fragments or details without any central point.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need short, explicitly signalled lectures on accessible content. Pre-sessional work should include full lectures linked to note-taking and integrated writing tasks. For PGT students in fields where lectures argue cumulatively, practise identifying points that are built rather than announced.
reviewNotes: The coverage figures cited are estimates for general spoken English; lecture-specific coverage requirements may differ and depend on technical vocabulary.

guidance.summary: Lectures share many features of conversation (Biber, 2006), including personal narrative, humour and asides, and Young's (1994) phase model shows how such material sits among structuring and content phases. Asides may carry cultural references that are opaque to newcomers, a cross-cultural dimension of listening that Flowerdew and Miller (2005) include in their model. Teach learners to recognise departure and return, to judge an aside's purpose, and to protect the main thread in their notes, recognising that anecdotes often serve as memorable illustrations of key points.

activities.title: Thread and tangent
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract and draw a line for the main thread, branching off when the lecturer digresses
Note the words or voice changes that signalled departure and return
Decide whether each branch illustrated a main point or was incidental
activities.intendedInsight: Digressions are signalled and often have a purpose.
activities.rationale: Makes visible the movement between content phases and conversational material characteristic of lecture discourse.

activities.title: Does the reference matter?
learnerActions: Listen to an aside that uses humour or a cultural reference
Discuss in groups what knowledge it assumes
Decide whether it matters for understanding the point, and how they could find out if unsure
activities.intendedInsight: Missing some references is normal; the skill is judging whether it matters.
activities.rationale: Addresses the cross-cultural dimension of lecture listening described by Flowerdew and Miller (2005) without treating it as a deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Learners record anecdotes or jokes as main content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes devote space to the anecdote and omit the point it illustrated.
difficulties.response: After each anecdote ask 'Why did the lecturer tell this story?' and note the point, not the story.

difficulties.pattern: Learners lose the thread after a digression and do not recognise the return.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes stop or become fragmented after an aside.
difficulties.response: Teach return markers explicitly and suggest leaving a visible gap in notes during a digression, resuming with a heading when the lecturer returns.

difficulties.pattern: Learners feel excluded or anxious when they miss humour or cultural references.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reports of feeling lost; disengagement after jokes.
difficulties.response: Normalise the experience as something anyone new to a context meets, and avoid presenting any national style of humour as something learners lack.

diagnostic.task: Play a lecture extract with a 1-minute digression and ask for a three-sentence summary, then ask what the digression was for.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The summary keeps the main thread; the digression is identified and its function judged.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The main thread is captured but the digression is over-represented or its link is not seen.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The summary is dominated by the digression or breaks off at it.

guidance.contextNotes: Less a foundation priority than a pre-sessional and in-sessional one, where authentic and conversational lecturing styles are common. In discussion-led PGT modules, asides often carry disciplinary values and practitioner knowledge that are worth noticing.

guidance.summary: Biber (2006) found that stance expressions are frequent in university classroom teaching, so lecturers routinely signal evaluation as well as content. In speech, stance is carried jointly by lexis, the framing of reported views and prosody, and scepticism or irony may be carried largely by the voice. Flowerdew and Miller (2005) include a critical dimension in their model of second language listening. Link this topic to written stance work (Hyland, 2005), but foreground spoken-specific cues.

activities.title: Whose voice?
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture section that presents several positions
Note each position and label it reported, endorsed, questioned or rejected
Underline the words, or describe the delivery, that told them
activities.intendedInsight: Lecturers often present views they do not hold, and the cues that mark distance can be subtle.
activities.rationale: Applies the distinction between the speaker's own claims and attributed claims to speech, where prosody adds cues not available in writing.

activities.title: Same words, different stance
learnerActions: Hear the same sentence delivered neutrally, approvingly and sceptically
Identify the stance each conveys and the vocal cues involved
Find a similar moment in a lecture recording and discuss it
activities.intendedInsight: Delivery can qualify or even reverse the literal meaning.
activities.rationale: Makes prosodic stance cues noticeable for learners who attend mainly to words; relates to the critical dimension of listening in Flowerdew and Miller (2005).

difficulties.pattern: Learners take every statement in a lecture as the lecturer's own view or as established fact, a pattern common among new university students of all backgrounds, especially where earlier courses presented content as settled knowledge.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes and later essays attribute to the lecturer positions the lecturer reported in order to criticise them.
difficulties.response: Teach spoken reporting frames (some people would argue…, the standard view is…) and make explicit that lecturers often present positions in order to evaluate them; this is a convention of the genre that new students need to learn.

difficulties.pattern: Ironic or sceptical delivery is missed and the literal meaning recorded.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes record ironic remarks as straightforward claims.
difficulties.response: Contrast literal and ironic delivery of the same sentence and flag irony when it occurs in class recordings.

diagnostic.task: After a 3-minute extract presenting a debate, ask: 'Which view does the lecturer favour, and what makes you think so?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the favoured view correctly and cites both lexical and prosodic cues.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the favoured view from lexical cues only, or partly confuses reported and endorsed views.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish the lecturer's view from the views reported.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG courses can introduce stance in lectures alongside written stance; on pre-sessional PG courses it is a core listening skill because lectures and seminars present contested positions from the start. PGT and PGR students in the social sciences and humanities meet lectures and seminars in which stance on contested theory is central; in STEM fields stance more often concerns the certainty of findings and evaluation of methods.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no source specifically on prosodic cues to stance or irony in L2 lecture listening; the prosodic claims are general and could be strengthened with a verified source.

guidance.summary: Basturkmen (2002) showed that meaning in seminar discussion is negotiated across several turns and speakers rather than in neat question–answer exchanges, and Basturkmen (2003) found that interaction patterns change when a tutor joins a student discussion. Subject lecturers also expect students to participate in class discussion (Ferris & Tagg, 1996), which requires following it first. Following such talk means tracking participants and their positions as well as content. Use authentic or realistic recordings of student discussion and link listening tasks directly to preparation for participation.

activities.title: Discussion map
learnerActions: Listen to a recorded seminar extract
Draw participants as nodes and arrows showing who responds to whom
Label each arrow (agrees, challenges, extends, asks)
Compare maps and replay disputed sections
activities.intendedInsight: Discussion has structure, built from relationships between turns.
activities.rationale: Reflects Basturkmen's (2002) finding that meaning in seminars is co-constructed across turns.

activities.title: Tutor in, tutor out
learnerActions: Compare two short recordings of a group discussion, with and without a tutor
Note differences in who speaks, turn length and how ideas are developed
Discuss what each pattern means for following and joining in
activities.intendedInsight: Discussion dynamics vary with participants and roles.
activities.rationale: Based on Basturkmen's (2003) comparison of discussion with and without the tutor present.

difficulties.pattern: Learners concentrate on decoding each speaker and lose track of how contributions relate.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report fragments of content but not who said what or how contributions connected.
difficulties.response: Use mapping tasks and set a second listening focused on relationships rather than content.

difficulties.pattern: Peers' varied accents, overlapping talk and fast exchanges lead learners to disengage.
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence in discussions; comments such as 'I couldn't follow, so I couldn't speak'.
difficulties.response: Build exposure gradually, and teach confirmation checks as legitimate participation. Avoid treating speed of response as the measure of good participation.

diagnostic.task: Play a 3-minute discussion and ask: 'What was the disagreement, and who was on each side?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the disagreement accurately and attributes positions correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the topic and some positions, with misattribution.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify any disagreement or attribute positions.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should include listening to recorded seminars before learners lead their own. In UG and PGT programmes with assessed participation this is a priority. PGR students face research group meetings and conference question sessions with faster, more specialised exchanges. Overlapping talk is particularly hard for deaf and hard-of-hearing students and for some autistic students; turn-taking ground rules, live captions and a shared written record of the discussion make following it accessible, and should be treated as normal practice rather than special treatment.

guidance.summary: Multimedia learning research suggests that learning from words and pictures depends on how the two are coordinated, and that on-screen text duplicating speech can compete for attention (Mayer, 2009). Rowley-Jolivet (2002) showed how central visuals are to scientific conference presentations, and the same holds for many lectures. For L2 listeners, decoding speech competes with reading slides, so teach them to use slides for orientation and speech for content, to annotate rather than copy, and to resolve spoken references to visuals.

activities.title: Slide plus
learnerActions: Receive a slide deck before a recorded lecture section
While listening, add only information that is said but not shown
Compare annotations with a partner to see what each captured
activities.intendedInsight: The value of attending a lecture lies largely in what is said beyond the slides.
activities.rationale: Directs attention to the spoken channel and away from reading text the speaker is also saying, the redundancy problem Mayer (2009) describes.

activities.title: Follow the pointer
learnerActions: Watch a lecturer explain a graph or diagram
Pause at each spoken reference (this, here, that peak) and point to the element meant
Give a short spoken explanation of the figure to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken references to visuals only work if the listener tracks both channels.
activities.rationale: Visual discourse is integral to academic presentation (Rowley-Jolivet, 2002); practising reference resolution is intended to build integration of the two channels.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read slides in full while the lecturer speaks and miss what is said.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes reproduce slide text; spoken explanations and examples are absent.
difficulties.response: Encourage reading slides before the lecture so that listening can take priority during it; annotate rather than copy.

difficulties.pattern: Learners cannot match spoken references to features of a graph because the graph type is unfamiliar.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion when the lecturer refers to axes, trends or regions of a diagram.
difficulties.response: Pre-teach the relevant graph conventions and trend vocabulary, and review the visuals before the lecture.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a slide containing a graph and play the lecturer's 1-minute explanation of it; ask them to annotate the slide with what was said about each feature.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Annotations are linked to the correct features and include spoken-only content.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some correct links, but annotations largely repeat what is already on the slide.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot link speech to the visual; annotations are absent or copied.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level, integrate this with graph reading and data commentary. In-sessionally, slides from students' own modules allow practice with real materials. Disciplines differ: some lectures are equation- or board-led, others rely on image or text slides. Spoken references such as 'this curve here' exclude blind and partially sighted students; teachers can model verbal description of visuals, which can also help every listener.
reviewNotes: Mayer's principles derive largely from experiments with first-language learners; their application to L2 lecture listening is an extrapolation.

guidance.summary: Recordings give L2 listeners the control over pace and repetition that live lectures lack, and captions can support listening comprehension and vocabulary learning (Montero Perez et al., 2013). Recordings are also easily used for low-utility study: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate rereading as low in utility, and passive rewatching is analogous. Lynch (2011) reviews the growing role of technology in academic listening. Teach learners to mark gaps during the live lecture, replay selectively, verify automatic captions, and turn what they review into retrieval practice.

activities.title: Mark, replay, repair
learnerActions: During a live or simulated lecture, mark moments of difficulty in notes with a symbol and approximate time
Afterwards, replay only those sections, with captions if helpful
Complete the notes and write one question to test themselves on later
activities.intendedInsight: Targeted replay is quicker and more useful than rewatching everything.
activities.rationale: Combines monitoring during listening with retrieval practice afterwards, rather than passive rewatching, which resembles the low-utility rereading discussed by Dunlosky et al. (2013).

activities.title: Check the captions
learnerActions: Watch a short lecture section with automatic captions
Identify caption errors on technical terms and names using the slides or reading
Discuss when captions help and when they mislead
activities.intendedInsight: Automatic captions are a useful but fallible support.
activities.rationale: Captions can support L2 listening (Montero Perez et al., 2013), but automatic captions are often unreliable for specialist terms and names.

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll watch the recording later' — and then either does not, or rewatches everything passively.
difficulties.revealedBy: A growing backlog of unwatched recordings; notes no better after rewatching.
difficulties.response: Agree a specific replay plan with time limits and targets. Avoid suggesting recordings as a remedy for every listening problem.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read captions as a text and stop listening.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comprehension drops sharply when captions are removed.
difficulties.response: Alternate captioned and uncaptioned replays, using captions to check rather than to follow. This advice is for listening practice only: for deaf and hard-of-hearing students, and some students with auditory processing differences, captions and transcripts are an access requirement and should never be withdrawn.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain how they would use the recording of a lecture they found difficult.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes targeted replay of marked sections, verification of terms and a time limit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Plans to rewatch the whole lecture, possibly with captions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Has no plan, or intends to rely on recordings instead of attending.

guidance.contextNotes: Many foundation and pre-sessional students meet lecture capture for the first time, so establish habits early. In UG and PGT programmes, recordings are most valuable for difficult lecturers and dense modules. Institutional recording policies and caption quality vary.
reviewNotes: Evidence on how lecture capture relates to attendance and attainment is mixed and not represented in the bibliography.

guidance.summary: Biber (2006) found that university classroom talk contains a substantial amount of procedural and directive language, and Biber et al. (2004) identified directive bundles (for example I want you to) among those frequent in classroom teaching. Obligation is often expressed indirectly or with hedging, so learners must interpret the strength of an instruction as well as its content. Teach learners to turn spoken instructions into checklists, to query conditions and deadlines, and to verify against written sources.

activities.title: Briefing to checklist
learnerActions: Listen to an assignment briefing
Write a checklist of requirements and deadlines
Compare with the written brief and identify discrepancies or information given only orally
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken briefings often add to or clarify the written brief.
activities.rationale: Links real-time listening to an action outcome using the kind of procedural talk Biber (2006) found common in university settings.

activities.title: Must, should or might?
learnerActions: Listen to extracts containing directives of varying strength
Rank them from obligatory to optional
Discuss which indirect forms nevertheless signal obligation
activities.intendedInsight: Indirect phrasing can still carry strong obligation.
activities.rationale: Directive bundles in classroom teaching often take indirect forms (Biber et al., 2004).

difficulties.pattern: Learners interpret hedged directives (you might want to look at…) as genuinely optional suggestions.
difficulties.revealedBy: Required preparation or tasks are missed after briefings phrased indirectly.
difficulties.response: Make explicit the force of common indirect directives in academic settings and encourage checking with the lecturer when the strength is unclear.

difficulties.pattern: Learners rely on peers' messages for instructions rather than checking official sources.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in deadlines or formats traced to second-hand information.
difficulties.response: Teach a verification routine using the learning platform and course handbook after every briefing.

difficulties.pattern: Institutional terms in briefings (extension, extenuating or mitigating circumstances, resit or make-up examination, submission point) are misunderstood, and the terms and procedures differ between institutions and countries.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners act on a briefing but misapply a procedure, for example confusing an extension with extenuating circumstances.
difficulties.response: Pre-teach the institutional vocabulary of the learners' own programme and target context, and check it in context.

diagnostic.task: Play a 1-minute laboratory safety briefing and ask the learner to list the steps in order and any prohibitions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All steps are listed in order and all prohibitions identified.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most steps are listed, but the order or conditions are confused.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Key steps or prohibitions are missing.

guidance.contextNotes: Particularly important at foundation level, where students are new to institutional procedures, and for practical disciplines with laboratories, studios or fieldwork. Pre-sessional courses can use real briefings for the course's own assessments. Spoken-only briefings disadvantage deaf and hard-of-hearing students and students who process speech slowly; encourage lecturers to provide the same information in writing.

guidance.summary: Recorded academic media combine features of lectures and conversation and are often less explicitly structured than lectures, with interview and panel formats that require tracking several speakers. Lynch (2011) notes that technology is changing how students encounter academic listening. Treat media as sources to be evaluated and cited, not only as listening practice, and exploit the control that recordings give listeners (replay, transcripts, speed adjustment) as Rost (2011) discusses for self-directed listening.

activities.title: Podcast as source
learnerActions: Choose a podcast episode or recorded talk relevant to an assignment topic
Evaluate its credibility using a short checklist (speaker, affiliation, evidence, date)
Take timestamped notes on relevant content
Write a short paraphrase of one point with a citation that includes a timestamp
activities.intendedInsight: Audio sources can be used and cited like written ones, with the same critical scrutiny.
activities.rationale: Integrates listening with source evaluation and citation, which are usually taught only for written sources.

activities.title: Who said what on the panel?
learnerActions: Listen to a recorded academic interview or panel discussion
Note each speaker's main contribution
Identify where speakers agree or disagree and with whom
activities.intendedInsight: Recorded discussions require the same tracking of speakers and positions as live seminars.
activities.rationale: Extends work on following multi-party talk to recorded media, where the listener can replay to check attribution.

difficulties.pattern: Learners treat any podcast or video as authoritative because it sounds expert.
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments cite popular or promotional audio sources without evaluation.
difficulties.response: Apply the source-evaluation criteria used for written sources, and compare an academic and a popular treatment of the same topic.

difficulties.pattern: Learners listen to whole episodes without a focus and cannot later locate relevant content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes are long and untargeted; no timestamps.
difficulties.response: Set a question before listening, use chapter markers and transcripts, and record timestamps as part of note-taking.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner a 10-minute section of an academic podcast and a question; ask for relevant points with timestamps and a credibility judgement.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Relevant points with accurate timestamps and a reasoned credibility judgement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Relevant points but no timestamps, or a credibility judgement based only on impression.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Untargeted notes and no evaluation.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce academic media as optional sources for projects. In UG and PGT programmes they are increasingly set as module materials. PGR students use recorded talks and podcasts to keep up with their field and should cite them accurately.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no source specifically on L2 learners' use of academic podcasts or recorded talks; this guidance is practice-based.

guidance.summary: Kiewra (1985) distinguished the encoding function of note-taking from the external-storage function and argued that reviewing notes typically contributes more to achievement than taking them. This framing helps learners see why notes must be organised and complete enough to use later, and why condensing ideas in one's own words matters. Mueller and Oppenheimer's (2014) finding that more verbatim note-taking was associated with poorer conceptual performance illustrates the encoding point, although Morehead et al. (2019) did not replicate its central claims about laptops robustly (see digital notes).

activities.title: Notes a week later
learnerActions: Take notes on a short lecture
A week later, without re-listening, use the notes to answer questions on the lecture
Identify what in the notes helped and where they failed
activities.intendedInsight: Notes must work as a record for a future self who has forgotten the lecture.
activities.rationale: Makes the external-storage function concrete (Kiewra, 1985).

activities.title: Transcribe or transform
learnerActions: Take notes on one short extract by writing down as much as possible word for word
Take notes on a second, comparable extract in own words and structure
Compare what can be recalled and explained from each
activities.intendedInsight: How notes are taken affects how deeply the content is processed.
activities.rationale: Illustrates the encoding function discussed by Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014); as a classroom demonstration it is not a controlled test, and outcomes will vary.

difficulties.pattern: 'Notes are for remembering what the lecturer said, so the more I write the better.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense, near-verbatim notes that learners themselves cannot use for revision.
difficulties.response: Use the 'notes a week later' activity to show that structure and selection matter more than volume.

difficulties.pattern: Learners take notes conscientiously but rarely look at them again until just before an examination.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes are unread between lecture and examination; learners report that notes 'don't help'.
difficulties.response: Build short review tasks into the course and link them explicitly to the storage function and to retrieval practice.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What are your notes for?' and 'When do you use them after the lecture?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Mentions both processing during note-taking and use afterwards, and describes regular use.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions keeping a record but not processing or regular use.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Takes notes out of habit with no later use, or takes no notes.

guidance.contextNotes: Most useful at foundation and pre-sessional level as the rationale for later note-taking work. Revisit briefly in-sessionally when students' notes are not supporting their revision.

guidance.summary: Selective notes in the note-taker's own words involve more processing than transcription and are more usable as a record (Kiewra, 1985), but learners need explicit criteria for selection. EAP guidance has long treated note-taking as a teachable study skill (Jordan, 1997). Link selection criteria to purpose and to signals in the input: structure, relevance markers, definitions and repetition.

activities.title: Purpose-driven notes
learnerActions: Take notes on the same text for two different stated purposes
Compare the two sets of notes
Explain why the content differs
activities.intendedInsight: There is no single correct set of notes; selection depends on purpose.
activities.rationale: Makes selection decisions explicit and connects them to the later use of notes.

activities.title: Note audit
learnerActions: Exchange notes with a peer
Highlight main ideas in one colour and detail in another
Discuss whether the balance suits the purpose and what could be cut
activities.intendedInsight: Selection can be evaluated and improved.
activities.rationale: Peer comparison makes differences in selection visible without a single model answer.

difficulties.pattern: Learners try to write everything down.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long notes with no hierarchy; key points buried among detail.
difficulties.response: Practise identifying main ideas first in reading, then transfer the criteria to listening; set word limits for notes on short inputs.

difficulties.pattern: Learners note content words but lose the relationships between ideas (cause, contrast, condition).
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes list topics, and a reconstruction from the notes misrepresents how the ideas were connected.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to reconstruct the argument from their notes; introduce arrows and relation symbols to record links.

diagnostic.task: Give a short text and a purpose; ask for notes in 5 minutes, then ask the learner to explain why they included each item.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notes are selective, relevant to the purpose and hierarchically organised, with reasons for inclusion.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notes contain the main ideas but also much unnecessary detail.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Notes are near-verbatim copying or a random selection of details.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, use short, clearly structured texts and lectures. Pre-sessional courses should vary purposes and input length. In-sessionally, use students' real reading and lecture notes.

guidance.summary: Abbreviation saves time, but the time saved is only valuable if the notes remain usable when reviewed (Kiewra, 1985). Teaching should emphasise a small, consistent system over long symbol lists, with priority on symbols for logical relations because they preserve reasoning. Many learners already use shorthand or words from other languages in notes, which is a legitimate resource as long as notes remain decodable and key terms are recorded in the form they will need later.

activities.title: Build a personal key
learnerActions: Review a set of conventional symbols and abbreviations
Choose about ten, and add abbreviations for five frequent terms in their subject
Use the key in a note-taking task and revise it afterwards
activities.intendedInsight: A small, consistent system is more useful than many ad hoc abbreviations.
activities.rationale: Practice-based guidance on note-taking shorthand of the kind found in EAP study-skills materials (Jordan, 1997).

activities.title: Notes to prose
learnerActions: Exchange notes with a peer
Rewrite one section in full sentences
Check the rewrite against the original source
activities.intendedInsight: Shorthand must be decodable, including by one's future self.
activities.rationale: Tests the storage function of notes directly.

difficulties.pattern: Learners believe notes must be entirely in English and avoid using their first language or other shorthand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners slow down to find English wording while the lecture moves on.
difficulties.response: Treat mixed-language notes as legitimate if they are decodable, while making sure key terms are recorded in English for later use in writing.

difficulties.pattern: Learners invent abbreviations on the spot that they cannot decode later.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot reconstruct parts of their own notes after a few days.
difficulties.response: Keep a running key at the front of each notebook or file, and review notes within a day.

difficulties.pattern: Conventional abbreviations are confused, for example e.g. used where i.e. is meant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes and later writing that list an example where a restatement was intended, or vice versa.
difficulties.response: Teach the meanings of the most common Latin abbreviations with examples and check them in learners' notes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to take notes on a 2-minute extract and then, two days later, read their notes aloud as full sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Reads back fluently and accurately, including logical relations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recovers content but some relations or abbreviations are unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot reconstruct significant parts of the notes.

guidance.contextNotes: Mainly a foundation and pre-sessional topic. In-sessionally, subject-specific abbreviations become more important and can be built into students' own keys.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography evaluates abbreviation systems empirically; this guidance is practice-based.

guidance.summary: Nesbit and Adesope's (2006) meta-analysis found that studying or constructing concept maps was associated with somewhat better retention and transfer than several comparison activities, with effects varying across conditions. The Cornell format (Pauk & Owens, 2014) builds review into the page through cue and summary areas. No format is universally superior; teach a small repertoire and the principle of matching format to the structure of the content and to the notes' later use.

activities.title: Same content, three formats
learnerActions: Take notes on a short lecture or text as an outline
Convert the notes into a table or concept map
Compare which relationships each format makes visible
activities.intendedInsight: Different formats foreground different relationships.
activities.rationale: Concept mapping that labels relations between ideas is associated with learning gains in Nesbit and Adesope's (2006) meta-analysis; the activity uses mapping as one option rather than a universal solution.

activities.title: Cornell review cycle
learnerActions: Take lecture notes in the main column
Within a day, write cue questions in the margin and a summary at the foot
Cover the main column and answer the cue questions from memory
activities.intendedInsight: A format can build review and self-testing into note-taking.
activities.rationale: Combines the Cornell layout with retrieval practice, which improves retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).

difficulties.pattern: 'Mind maps suit me because I'm a visual learner.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners use one format for all content regardless of its structure.
difficulties.response: Present format choice as matching content structure and purpose. Do not endorse matching formats to 'learning styles', a claim that lacks good evidential support.

difficulties.pattern: Learners spend so long on layout during a lecture that they miss content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Carefully drawn but incomplete notes.
difficulties.response: Use simple linear formats during the lecture and rework the notes into maps or tables during review.

diagnostic.task: Give a short comparison text and ask the learner to choose a format and make notes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Chooses a table or matrix with criteria and explains why.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Uses an outline that captures the content but obscures the comparison.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies sentences with no organising format.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from explicit modelling of two or three formats. Pre-sessional courses can link tables and matrices to synthesis tasks. PGT students may extend matrices into literature synthesis grids.

guidance.summary: Lecture note-taking places heavy simultaneous demands on L2 listeners, as decoding, selecting and writing compete for attention. Kiewra (1985) emphasises that complete notes and review of them are associated with better learning, and research on L2 lecture comprehension and note-taking is collected in Flowerdew (1994). Teach note-taking with authentic lectures, linking discourse cues (previews, macro-markers, which Chaudron and Richards (1986) found aided recall, and relevance markers) to note structure, and build in post-lecture completion.

activities.title: Structure-first notes
learnerActions: Before the lecture, set up headings from the preview or slides
During the lecture, add points under the headings, starring content the lecturer flags
After the lecture, compare notes with a partner and fill gaps
activities.intendedInsight: A frame prepared in advance frees attention for content during the lecture.
activities.rationale: Uses macro-structure, which supports recall (Chaudron & Richards, 1986), as the organising frame for notes.

activities.title: Notes to summary
learnerActions: Take notes on a lecture
Write a summary using only the notes
Check the summary against the recording and identify gaps in the notes
activities.intendedInsight: The test of notes is what they let you do afterwards.
activities.rationale: Tests the storage function of notes (Kiewra, 1985) and links note-taking to summary writing.

difficulties.pattern: Learners try to write everything and lose the thread of the lecture.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes are detailed for the first minutes and then break off.
difficulties.response: Practise selecting main points in short segments before extending to full lectures; leave marked gaps rather than falling behind.

difficulties.pattern: Learners copy slide text and miss the spoken explanation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes duplicate the slides almost exactly.
difficulties.response: Provide slides in advance and ask learners to annotate them only with what is said.

difficulties.pattern: Learners stop to work out the spelling of unfamiliar terms and fall behind.
difficulties.revealedBy: Gaps in notes immediately after new terminology.
difficulties.response: Encourage approximate spelling marked with a query, checked afterwards against slides or readings.

diagnostic.task: Collect notes from a 15-minute lecture and ask the learner to explain the lecture's structure from the notes.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The notes show the structure clearly and the explanation is accurate.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Main points are present but the structure is unclear or flagged content is missing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Notes are fragmentary and the lecture cannot be reconstructed from them.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners benefit from guided note frames. Pre-sessional UG courses should use full-length lectures with integrated writing tasks that require the notes; pre-sessional PG courses can use denser lectures and link notes to seminar preparation. In-sessionally, review students' own notes from their modules. Some students (for example deaf students, or students with dyslexia or motor difficulties) work with a human note-taker, recordings or assistive technology; assess what they do with notes, such as selection and summary, rather than real-time handwriting speed.

guidance.summary: Pecorari (2003) showed that much L2 textual borrowing takes the form of patchwriting without intent to deceive, and Shi (2004) found more unattributed borrowing in summary tasks than in opinion tasks, and more among L2 than L1 writers in her sample. Reading notes are where source wording and one's own wording most easily become confused, so note-making routines are a practical point of intervention (Pecorari, 2013). Teach a layout that physically separates quotation, own-words notes and comment, with page numbers recorded at the time of writing.

activities.title: Three-column notes
learnerActions: Divide the page or file into three columns: exact words with page number, own-words notes, own comments and questions
Make notes on a short article using all three columns
Swap with a peer and check that each column contains only what it should
activities.intendedInsight: Separating source words, source ideas and one's own ideas at the note stage is intended to prevent confusion later.
activities.rationale: A practical routine reflecting Pecorari's (2013) emphasis on teaching source use rather than only policing plagiarism.

activities.title: Read, cover, write
learnerActions: Read a paragraph carefully
Cover it and write notes from memory in own words
Uncover and check for accuracy and for unintended copying
activities.intendedInsight: Writing notes away from the text is intended to reduce copying and to test understanding.
activities.rationale: Targets the close textual dependence described as patchwriting by Pecorari (2003).

difficulties.pattern: 'I'll remember which parts I copied.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Assignments that include unmarked source wording traced to the student's own notes.
difficulties.response: Show how copied wording in notes later reappears unmarked in drafts; require quotation marks and page numbers at the moment of copying.

difficulties.pattern: Learners copy key sentences because they feel they cannot express the idea better than the author.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes consist mostly of copied sentences, some unmarked.
difficulties.response: Treat this as a developmental stage rather than a moral failing; support with read-cover-write and with paraphrasing practice, and allow marked quotation in notes.

difficulties.pattern: Learners omit source details and page numbers and cannot find them later.
difficulties.revealedBy: Time lost re-finding sources; citations without page numbers for quotations.
difficulties.response: Make a source header with full details and a page column non-negotiable features of every set of notes.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to show notes from a recent reading and point out which parts are quotations, which are their own words and which are their own ideas.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All three are clearly and consistently distinguished, with page numbers and source details.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some distinction is made but inconsistently, or page numbers are missing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No distinction is made, or the learner cannot tell which parts were copied.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, model and check the layout closely. Pre-sessional courses should link it to source-based writing assessments, with PG courses using longer and more numerous sources. In-sessional UG and PGT students reading for assignments and dissertations need the same separation in digital form, often within reference management software, as do PGR students managing a large literature.

guidance.summary: Kiewra (1985) emphasised review as a key function of notes. Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated practice testing and distributed practice as high-utility learning techniques and rereading, highlighting and summarisation as lower utility; retrieval practice improves long-term retention (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) and spacing helps (Cepeda et al., 2006). Reviewing notes is therefore best organised around self-testing at intervals, with summarising used to repair and consolidate notes rather than as the main review activity.

activities.title: Cover and recall
learnerActions: Write three to five questions in the margin of a set of notes
Cover the notes and answer the questions from memory
Check answers and mark items for further review
activities.intendedInsight: Retrieving information from memory strengthens learning more than rereading it.
activities.rationale: Applies retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) to notes.

activities.title: Spaced review calendar
learnerActions: Plan short reviews of each lecture's notes after one day, one week and one month
Record the result of each self-test
Adjust the schedule for topics that remain difficult
activities.intendedInsight: Spacing review over time supports retention better than cramming.
activities.rationale: Applies distributed practice (Cepeda et al., 2006; Dunlosky et al., 2013).

difficulties.pattern: Learners recopy notes neatly or reread them and feel they have learnt them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report hours of review but perform poorly on recall questions.
difficulties.response: Contrast rereading with self-testing in a short class experiment and discuss the difference between familiarity and recall.

difficulties.pattern: Self-testing feels uncomfortable because it exposes what has been forgotten.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners abandon self-testing after a few attempts.
difficulties.response: Explain that the effort of retrieval is part of what makes it effective, and keep early self-tests short and low-stakes.

difficulties.pattern: Learners leave all review until the examination period.
difficulties.revealedBy: No review activity during the term; heavy cramming before examinations.
difficulties.response: Build short weekly review into the course schedule and check it.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner how they would prepare from their notes for a test in two weeks.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes spaced self-testing from questions generated from the notes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes rereading or summarising, with some spacing.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans to reread everything the night before.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses can model review with course content. In UG and PGT programmes, link review to module assessment schedules and to examination preparation.

guidance.summary: Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) reported that laptop note-takers wrote more verbatim notes and performed worse on conceptual questions than longhand note-takers. Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson (2019) replicated and extended the study and did not find robust differences, concluding that the evidence does not justify strong claims for longhand superiority. Sana, Weston and Cepeda (2013) found that laptop multitasking harmed learning for users and for nearby peers. Both note-taking studies tested first-language English undergraduates watching short talks in laboratory conditions, so their transfer to L2 lecture note-taking is untested. Present this as an open debate: the defensible advice is to avoid verbatim transcription and multitasking whatever the device, and never to require handwriting where students rely on typed notes or assistive technology.

activities.title: Read the debate
learnerActions: Read the abstracts of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) and Morehead et al. (2019)
Summarise what each study claims and how they differ
Decide in groups what advice the evidence actually supports
activities.intendedInsight: Popular claims about research should be checked against the studies, including replications.
activities.rationale: Uses a live replication debate to model critical reading of evidence, while addressing the practical question directly.

activities.title: Device audit
learnerActions: For one week, record for each lecture which device was used, any distractions and how much of the notes was verbatim
Use the notes for a short self-test
Reflect on what to change
activities.intendedInsight: How a device is used matters more than which device is used.
activities.rationale: Makes multitasking and verbatim transcription visible to the learner (Sana et al., 2013).

difficulties.pattern: 'Research proves handwriting is better.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners repeat the claim from popular sources, sometimes against their own needs.
difficulties.response: Show the replication results and focus on processing rather than device.

difficulties.pattern: Learners type quickly and transcribe almost verbatim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Typed notes that read like a transcript.
difficulties.response: Set word limits per lecture section or require condensed headings and summaries.
