difficulties.pattern: Notes are scattered across apps, devices and cloud services and cannot be found later.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners cannot locate notes for a given lecture or source.
difficulties.response: Agree a simple filing system linked to modules and dates, with regular backup.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner which method they use and why, and to retrieve their notes from a specific lecture two weeks ago.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A reasoned choice that represents the evidence accurately; notes are found quickly and are processed rather than verbatim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Choice based on habit; notes found but largely verbatim.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats myths, cannot find notes, or notes are absent.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional students often arrive with established habits; address the evidence early. In UG and PGT programmes, practical organisation becomes more important as volume grows. Students with dyslexia, dyspraxia or other disabilities may rely on typed notes, dictation, recording or assistive software; guidance should never imply that handwriting is required.
reviewNotes: Review response: the laptop–longhand evidence is presented as contested (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014; Morehead et al., 2019), with the limits of laboratory and first-language samples stated; no device recommendation is made.

guidance.summary: Kiewra's (1985) distinction between encoding and external storage suggests that shared notes can supply the storage function but not the processing benefit of taking notes oneself, so students who rely only on others' notes miss that processing. Collaborative notes are probably most useful as a supplement to individual notes, through comparison, correction and pooling of gaps. Institutional rules on collusion (Bretag, 2016) mean students need to know where sharing notes ends and sharing assessed work begins. In multilingual groups, attention to equitable division of work matters.

activities.title: Compare, correct, combine
learnerActions: Take individual notes on a lecture
In groups, compare notes and mark disagreements
Check disagreements against the recording and produce a corrected shared version
activities.intendedInsight: Comparison exposes errors and gaps that individuals miss.
activities.rationale: Preserves individual processing while gaining the storage benefits of pooled notes, following Kiewra's (1985) distinction.

activities.title: Where is the line?
learnerActions: Read short scenarios about sharing notes and drafts
Decide whether each is permitted collaboration or collusion under the institution's policy
Discuss borderline cases
activities.intendedInsight: Sharing notes is usually acceptable; sharing assessed work usually is not.
activities.rationale: Applies institutional integrity policy to a common study practice.

difficulties.pattern: Some group members rely entirely on others' notes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Group members cannot explain content without the shared notes.
difficulties.response: Rotate responsibilities and require each member to add summaries or questions.

difficulties.pattern: Errors in shared notes spread to everyone who uses them.
difficulties.revealedBy: The same misconception appears across several students' work.
difficulties.response: Build in a checking role and verification against sources.

difficulties.pattern: Learners are unsure whether sharing notes for an assessed task is allowed.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about collusion; very similar submitted work.
difficulties.response: Clarify institutional rules with concrete examples.

diagnostic.task: Ask a group to describe how they share notes and what they would do if asked to share notes for an assessed essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes a structured process with checking and individual contribution, and an accurate understanding of collusion rules.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Shares notes informally without checking; vague on rules.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Copies others' notes wholesale; unaware of collusion risks.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can model collaborative notes with clear rules. UG and PGT students often form study groups independently; in-sessional support can address integrity and effectiveness together.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no empirical source on collaborative note-taking; guidance relies on reasoning from Kiewra's functions and on practice.

guidance.summary: Munro and Derwing (1995) showed that accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility are related but partly independent: speech can be strongly accented yet fully intelligible. Levis (2005) contrasted the nativeness principle with the intelligibility principle and argued that instruction should prioritise features that affect understanding, and the CEFR Companion Volume's phonological scales were redeveloped around intelligibility rather than native-speaker norms (Council of Europe, 2020). Jenkins' (2000) Lingua Franca Core proposes intelligibility priorities for lingua franca settings, though its specific inventory is contested. Teaching should begin from what listeners actually fail to understand.

activities.title: Transcribe and rate
learnerActions: Record a 1-minute explanation of a concept from their field
Ask two listeners to transcribe a section and rate how easy it was to understand
Compare the transcriptions with the script and identify where understanding failed
Choose one or two features to work on based on the failures, not on accent
activities.intendedInsight: What matters is what listeners understand, which is not the same as how accented the speech sounds.
activities.rationale: Applies the intelligibility measures used by Munro and Derwing (1995) as a diagnostic.

activities.title: Accent is not the problem
learnerActions: Listen to several speakers with different accents explaining academic concepts
Rate each for accent strength and ease of understanding
Discuss cases where a strong accent was easy to understand and why
activities.intendedInsight: Accent and ease of understanding are partly independent.
activities.rationale: Experiences the partial independence of accent and comprehensibility reported by Munro and Derwing (1995) and the intelligibility principle argued by Levis (2005).

difficulties.pattern: 'I need to lose my accent to be taken seriously.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Requests for accent reduction; anxiety about speaking in front of peers.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge that accent bias exists — Rubin (1992) found that listeners' expectations affected their comprehension of identical speech — while reframing goals around intelligibility and pointing out that listener attitudes are not the speaker's fault. Do not promise accent elimination or frame accent as a deficit.

difficulties.pattern: Learners equate good pronunciation with producing individual sounds correctly and neglect stress and prosody.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners ask only for work on particular sounds; their stress and prosody errors cause more misunderstanding than their sounds.
difficulties.response: Show evidence that stress and prominence affect intelligibility (Field, 2005; Hahn, 2004) and use listener transcription to locate actual breakdowns.

difficulties.pattern: Speaking criteria, feedback or listeners' comments reward 'native-like' pronunciation or penalise accent, so the learner is judged on accentedness rather than on how well they are understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rubrics with descriptors such as 'native-like' or 'neutral accent'; feedback that names the accent without identifying any misunderstanding; learners who are intelligible but receive low pronunciation marks.
difficulties.response: Assessment teams should review speaking criteria so that pronunciation is judged on intelligibility and comprehensibility for the intended audience, and train raters to separate accent from understanding. Learners can ask for feedback that names what a listener did not understand.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner: 'What would good pronunciation mean for you at university?' and 'Which parts of your pronunciation cause listeners problems?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines goals in terms of being understood by their audience and names specific features based on feedback.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mentions being understood but sets goals in terms of imitating a reference accent, or lists sounds without evidence.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Aims to eliminate accent and has no sense of which features matter.

guidance.contextNotes: This concept frames all pronunciation work and should be introduced at foundation and pre-sessional level, both UG and PG. In-sessionally it is revisited when students ask for accent reduction. For PGR students who teach or present internationally, it supports a confident professional identity as a multilingual speaker.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-01): stage roles now limit this topic to develop at foundation and pre-sessional stages and revisit elsewhere; it is not core at any stage because it is a framing concept rather than a separately assessed skill.

guidance.summary: Field (2005) found that misplaced lexical stress reduced intelligibility for both native and non-native listeners, with shifts to a later syllable especially disruptive in his data. Because stress shifts systematically across academic word families, and a limited number of stress patterns account for much of the Academic Word List (Murphy & Kandil, 2004), stress can be taught alongside vocabulary as part of knowing a word. Compound and phrase stress matter too: noun + noun compounds, which are frequent in technical vocabulary, usually stress the first element, whereas adjective + noun phrases stress the noun. Teach stress with each new word, emphasise patterns rather than lists, and check perception as well as production (Derwing & Munro, 2015).

activities.title: Word family stress patterns
learnerActions: Sort members of academic word families (analyse, analysis, analytical; economy, economic, economics) by which syllable is stressed
Infer rules associated with particular suffixes
Test the rules on new words using dictionary audio
activities.intendedInsight: Stress shifts follow patterns that can be learnt and used to predict new words.
activities.rationale: Draws on the regularity of stress patterns in academic vocabulary described by Murphy and Kandil (2004).

activities.title: Stress in vocabulary records
learnerActions: Add stress marking to vocabulary notes or cards for every new multi-syllable word
Practise saying each word within a common collocation
Test a partner on stress placement for recently learnt words
activities.intendedInsight: Stress is part of knowing a word, not an extra.
activities.rationale: Field (2005) shows that stress is part of what listeners use to recognise words, so learners need it stored with the word.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language has fixed stress, or little lexical stress contrast, apply one stress position to all words or give syllables similar weight.
difficulties.revealedBy: Consistent stress on the first or last syllable regardless of the word; few reduced vowels.
difficulties.response: Teach English stress as variable but patterned, and practise reduced vowels in unstressed syllables alongside stress placement.

difficulties.pattern: Learners keep the stress of the base word in derived forms (ANalysis by analogy with ANalyse).
difficulties.revealedBy: Stress errors concentrated in derived forms of familiar words.
difficulties.response: Present family members together and highlight the stress shift; practise in contrast.

difficulties.pattern: Learners have met most academic vocabulary through reading and have guessed its stress from spelling.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confident but consistently wrong stress on long words learnt through reading.
difficulties.response: Build checking with dictionary audio into vocabulary routines and treat stress as part of word knowledge.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud six academic words in two families and to mark the stress before saying them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Marks and produces stress correctly, including shifts, and explains the pattern.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct on base forms but errors on derived forms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify stressed syllables or produces most incorrectly.

guidance.contextNotes: Teach from foundation level onwards alongside vocabulary. In-sessionally and at PGR level, technical vocabulary from students' own fields provides the most useful material.

guidance.summary: Thought groups are the foundation of Gilbert's (2008) prosody pyramid: each group carries one focus word, and boundaries are marked by pitch change and pausing. Chunking speech at grammatical boundaries helps listeners parse it and gives speakers natural planning points, whereas pauses inside phrases make speech harder to follow. Derwing and Munro (2015) include prosodic features among those that matter for comprehensibility. Thought-group work transfers readily to presentations and to reading quotations or data aloud.

activities.title: Mark and read
learnerActions: Mark thought-group boundaries in a short academic paragraph with slashes
Read it aloud and record it
Listen back and compare the pauses with the marked boundaries
activities.intendedInsight: Planned chunks can make speech easier to follow and easier to produce.
activities.rationale: Applies Gilbert's (2008) thought-group principle to academic text.

activities.title: Chunk the dense sentence
learnerActions: Take a long academic sentence with heavy noun phrases
Divide it into thought groups for speaking
Discuss where a spoken version would need to differ from the written one
activities.intendedInsight: Dense written sentences need restructuring or careful chunking to be spoken intelligibly.
activities.rationale: Links thought groups to the difference between spoken and written academic language.

difficulties.pattern: Learners read aloud word by word, giving each word equal weight and pausing between many words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Monotonous, evenly paced reading, typical where reading aloud has been practised mainly as accurate word decoding.
difficulties.response: Model reading in thought groups and practise marking boundaries before reading; avoid correcting individual words while learners are working on chunking.

difficulties.pattern: Learners pause inside phrases while searching for the next word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mid-phrase pauses in spontaneous speech.
difficulties.response: Encourage planning in phrases rather than words, and link to formulaic chunks and fluency work.

difficulties.pattern: Learners break long academic noun phrases into single-word groups.
difficulties.revealedBy: Pauses inside noun phrases such as 'the long-term economic consequences of the policy'.
difficulties.response: Analyse the structure of noun phrases and practise saying them as units.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read a 60-word paragraph aloud without preparation, then again after marking thought groups.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Pauses at grammatical boundaries in both readings.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves markedly after marking boundaries.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Pauses inconsistently or word by word in both readings.

guidance.contextNotes: A foundation-level priority that remains useful at all stages. For PGT and PGR presenters, thought-group planning supports reading definitions, quotations and data aloud clearly.

guidance.summary: Hahn (2004) found that when a non-native speaker's lecture had correctly placed primary stress, listeners recalled more content and evaluated the speaker more favourably than when stress was misplaced or absent. Prominence links pronunciation to information structure: it tells listeners which word in a thought group carries the new or contrastive point. Nuclear stress placement is one of the few prosodic features Jenkins (2000) retained in the Lingua Franca Core, so prominence is a priority in lingua franca settings as well as elsewhere. Gilbert's (2008) prosody pyramid offers a teachable sequence from thought group to focus word to stressed syllable.

activities.title: Shifting focus
learnerActions: Read the same sentence as an answer to different questions
Move the prominence each time to the word that answers the question
Explain to a partner why it moved
activities.intendedInsight: Prominence goes to new or contrastive information, so it moves with context.
activities.rationale: Makes the link between prominence and information structure explicit, following Gilbert's (2008) focus-word approach.

activities.title: Contrast in explanation
learnerActions: Prepare a short explanation comparing two methods or theories from their field
Mark the contrastive words and practise them with prominence
Present to a peer, who notes which contrasts came across
activities.intendedInsight: Correct prominence makes comparisons and key points easier to follow.
activities.rationale: Applies Hahn's (2004) finding about primary stress and listener recall to academic explanation.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language marks focus mainly through word order, particles or syntax rather than pitch prominence do not use prominence to highlight new information, or stress every content word equally.
difficulties.revealedBy: Even stress across content words; contrasts not audible.
difficulties.response: Contrast versions with and without prominence in question–answer pairs and show how meaning changes; practise in short dialogues before extended speech. The spoken contrast can later be linked to given and new information in writing.

difficulties.pattern: Learners place prominence on the last word of every thought group regardless of whether it is new.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated or given words at the end of groups receive prominence.
difficulties.response: Practise de-accenting repeated words and moving focus to earlier new information.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer: 'Did the study use interviews or questionnaires?' with 'The study used questionnaires', then 'Did the first study use questionnaires?' with 'The second study used questionnaires'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Prominence moves correctly to 'questionnaires' and then to 'second'.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct in one case only.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No change in prominence between the two answers.

guidance.contextNotes: Introduce at foundation level with short exchanges; develop in pre-sessional presentation work. For PGR students who teach, prominence is especially relevant to clear explanation.
reviewNotes: Review response (R2-10): the edge from coh.given-new is soft and reworded, and this difficulty now returns to thought groups rather than to written information structure, so the spoken given–new contrast is taught through question–answer pairs without waiting for B2 written-discourse work.

guidance.summary: Pickering (2001), using Brazil's discourse intonation framework (Brazil, 1997), found that international teaching assistants used fewer rising (referring) tones than native-speaker teaching assistants, which may have made their teaching sound less interactive and made shared and new information harder to distinguish. Thompson (2003) showed that intonation contributes to signalling lecture organisation. Teach intonation through its discourse functions — new versus shared information, continuation versus completion, topic structure — rather than through attitude labels, which are unreliable.

activities.title: New or shared?
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract and mark falling and rising tones on a transcript
Decide whether each marked point is presented as new or as shared
Practise a short explanation using the same contrast
activities.intendedInsight: Tone choices signal how information relates to what listeners already know.
activities.rationale: Applies Brazil's (1997) distinction between proclaiming and referring tones, as used by Pickering (2001).

activities.title: Lists and transitions
learnerActions: Practise saying lists with continuing tones and a final fall
Practise topic transitions with a pitch reset
Record a short presentation section and check both features
activities.intendedInsight: Intonation signals structure to listeners.
activities.rationale: Links intonation to the signalling of organisation described by Thompson (2003).

difficulties.pattern: Learners use a narrower pitch range and fewer discourse-marking pitch movements in English than proficient speakers, a tendency reported across many first-language backgrounds and linked to processing load and unfamiliarity with English tone choices.
difficulties.revealedBy: Narrow pitch range; topic shifts and contrasts not signalled prosodically.
difficulties.response: Practise exaggerated pitch range in controlled tasks and then reduce it; record and listen back.

difficulties.pattern: 'Intonation is about showing emotion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners treat intonation as optional decoration.
difficulties.response: Show its discourse functions with academic examples, where it affects how organisation and information status come across.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read a short list and a sentence that refers back to earlier content.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses continuing and final tones on the list and a referring tone on given information.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gets list intonation right but does not distinguish given and new.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Uses flat or uniformly falling intonation throughout.

guidance.contextNotes: Most relevant from pre-sessional level onwards. Particularly important for PGR students who teach, given Pickering's (2001) findings about teaching assistants' tone choices.

guidance.summary: Munro and Derwing (2006) found that errors in high-functional-load contrasts had a greater effect on comprehensibility than errors in low-functional-load contrasts. Jenkins (2000) proposed a Lingua Franca Core of features, including most consonant contrasts and vowel length, as priorities for intelligibility in lingua franca settings, while excluding features such as the dental fricatives, weak forms, word stress and pitch movement (nuclear stress placement is one of the few prosodic features it retains, which supports the priority given to prominence); the core has been influential but is contested, for example over its empirical base and its treatment of word stress. Derwing and Munro (2015) summarise evidence that instruction can improve pronunciation. Prioritise individually, on the basis of what listeners actually misunderstand.

activities.title: Find my priorities
learnerActions: Record a short reading and a short spontaneous talk
Ask a listener unfamiliar with their first language to transcribe both
Identify words misunderstood and the sounds involved
Choose two priority features and plan practice
activities.intendedInsight: Priorities should be based on what listeners misunderstand, not on a generic list.
activities.rationale: Applies the intelligibility-based prioritisation argued by Derwing and Munro (2015).

activities.title: Minimal pairs in academic context
learnerActions: Practise a high-functional-load contrast in academic sentences from their field
Ask a partner to identify which word was intended
Record and monitor the target in a short presentation
activities.intendedInsight: Practice is most useful on contrasts that change meaning frequently.
activities.rationale: Targets high-functional-load contrasts, which Munro and Derwing (2006) found to matter more for comprehensibility.

activities.title: Perception training with many voices
learnerActions: Choose one priority contrast identified from listener transcription
Using a free high-variability training tool or a teacher-made set, identify which word of a pair is spoken, across many different talkers and word contexts, with immediate feedback
Track accuracy over several short sessions
Move on to producing the contrast in academic sentences once identification is reliable
activities.intendedInsight: Hearing a contrast reliably across many voices is a foundation for producing it.
activities.rationale: High-variability phonetic training (identification across many talkers with feedback) is a well-researched perception technique that has been associated with gains in perception and, in many studies, production (Thomson, 2018); perception-focused instruction is among the approaches reviewed by Thomson and Derwing (2015). Its use in EAP classes is a proposal rather than a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: Learners try to fix every sound and become discouraged.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frustration and low confidence; little progress on any feature.
difficulties.response: Limit targets to two or three high-priority features and track progress on those.

difficulties.pattern: Learners whose first language allows few word-final consonants or clusters delete final consonants or add a vowel after them, so that past tense and plural endings become inaudible.
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners mishear tense or number; final consonants missing in recordings.
difficulties.response: Practise grammatically meaningful endings in context, linking them to the next word where possible.

difficulties.pattern: Learners or previous teachers have focused on /θ/ and /ð/ at the expense of contrasts that matter more.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners request work on 'th' sounds but have more serious intelligibility issues elsewhere.
difficulties.response: Explain functional load and redirect effort, while respecting learners' own goals.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to name the sounds they think cause most misunderstanding, then compare with listener transcription.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names features that match listener evidence and explains why they matter.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names some correct features alongside low-priority ones.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Names only low-priority features or has no idea.

guidance.contextNotes: Most relevant at foundation and pre-sessional levels, where individual diagnosis can be built in. In-sessionally, work is usually individual and targeted at specific communicative needs.
reviewNotes: Specific contrasts named as high or low functional load are general tendencies; the exact ranking varies across studies.

Review response (R2-41): an HVPT activity has been added. Thomson (2018) is not in the closed bibliography and is listed under proposedReferences; if it is not accepted, cite the activity to thomsonderwing2015 only and soften the rationale.

guidance.summary: Recognising connected speech is clearly a priority for listening (Field, 2008); its value in production is more contested. Jenkins (2000) excluded weak forms from the Lingua Franca Core, arguing that they are not necessary for intelligibility in lingua franca communication and may even reduce it, whereas others argue that reducing unstressed words helps stressed information stand out for listeners accustomed to English rhythm (see Derwing & Munro, 2015, for discussion of priorities). A defensible middle course is moderate linking and reduction within thought groups, with content words kept clear.

activities.title: Script to speech
learnerActions: Mark linking and weak forms in a short presentation script
Practise reading with the marked features
Record and compare with an unmarked reading
activities.intendedInsight: Moderate linking makes speech flow without sacrificing clarity.
activities.rationale: Practice-based activity applying connected-speech features within thought groups.

activities.title: Chunk practice
learnerActions: Practise common presentation phrases as connected units
Use them in a short presentation
Peer-check that content words remain clear
activities.intendedInsight: Formulaic phrases are good candidates for connected delivery.
activities.rationale: Links connected speech to fluency through formulaic language.

difficulties.pattern: After learning about connected speech, learners over-reduce and blur content words.
difficulties.revealedBy: Key terms become hard to identify.
difficulties.response: Emphasise that reduction applies to unstressed function words; keep content words clear.

difficulties.pattern: Learners give every function word a full form and equal weight, so key words do not stand out for listeners used to English rhythm. Full forms are not in themselves an error, and many such speakers remain intelligible.
difficulties.revealedBy: Even rhythm and few reduced forms, together with listener reports of difficulty identifying the key points.
difficulties.response: Work on contrasting stressed and unstressed syllables, starting from recognition before production. Judge success by whether listeners can pick out the key words, not by how many weak forms the speaker uses.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read a 30-second presentation opening aloud.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Moderate linking and weak forms; content words clear.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Few reductions, but intelligible.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Listeners cannot pick out the key words, either because every syllable receives equal weight so that key words do not stand out or because over-reduction obscures content words.

guidance.contextNotes: Teach production after or alongside recognition. For presentation-focused PGT and PGR learners, emphasis should be on clarity of key terms and fluent formulaic phrases rather than maximal reduction.
reviewNotes: The production value of weak forms is contested; this record presents both positions without resolving them.

guidance.summary: Technical terms are often met first in reading, so learners form their pronunciation from spelling, which in English is an unreliable guide to stress. Because stress errors disrupt word recognition (Field, 2005) and key terms recur throughout an explanation, a mispronounced term can impair a whole presentation. Compound terms (CASE study, CONTROL group) follow compound stress patterns that learners can check in the same way. Teach a checking routine, prioritise the terms students will actually use, and accept that some names and terms have more than one accepted pronunciation (Derwing & Munro, 2015, on prioritising intelligibility).

activities.title: Presentation term check
learnerActions: List the ten most important terms and names in a forthcoming presentation
Check each using dictionary audio or a recording from the field
Mark stress and practise each term in a sentence
Ask a peer from the same field to confirm
activities.intendedInsight: Checking a few recurring key terms can make a noticeable difference to clarity.
activities.rationale: Applies Field's (2005) finding on stress and recognition to the terms that recur most in a talk.

activities.title: Acronym or initialism?
learnerActions: Sort a list of abbreviations from their field into those said as words and those said as letters
Check uncertain cases with a field-specific source
Practise them in context
activities.intendedInsight: Conventions for saying abbreviations vary and must be checked.
activities.rationale: Practice-based activity addressing a common source of uncertainty.

difficulties.pattern: Learners pronounce terms as spelled because they learnt them through reading.
difficulties.revealedBy: Systematic stress errors on technical terms.
difficulties.response: Build pronunciation checking into vocabulary learning from the start.

difficulties.pattern: International terms that are cognates in the learner's first language are given the first-language stress pattern.
difficulties.revealedBy: Familiar-looking terms are mispronounced more often than unfamiliar ones.
difficulties.response: Highlight cognates with different stress and practise them explicitly.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to say five key terms from their field and explain how they checked them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct stress and a reliable checking method.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Mostly correct but without a checking method.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent errors and reliance on spelling.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant at all stages. For PGR students presenting at conferences, names of theorists and specialised terms are particularly salient to expert audiences.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography addresses the pronunciation of technical terms directly; the claim relies on general findings about stress and intelligibility.

guidance.summary: Levelt's (1989) model of speaking includes a monitor that checks speech before and after articulation; in L2 speech, monitoring competes for attention with formulation, so selective monitoring matters. Dörnyei and Scott (1997) catalogue communication strategies such as circumlocution, approximation and appeals for help, which can be taught as legitimate ways of maintaining interaction. In academic speaking, the key judgement is which errors need repair: those that change meaning, especially in technical content.

activities.title: Explain without the word
learnerActions: Draw a card with a technical term from their field
Explain it to a partner without using the term
The partner guesses the term and comments on the clarity of the explanation
activities.intendedInsight: Paraphrase and description can carry meaning when a word is unavailable.
activities.rationale: Practises circumlocution and approximation as described by Dörnyei and Scott (1997).

activities.title: Repair or let go?
learnerActions: Listen to a recording of their own talk
Identify errors and decide which affected meaning
Practise brief repairs for meaning-affecting errors only
activities.intendedInsight: Not all errors need repairing.
activities.rationale: Develops selective monitoring in line with Levelt's (1989) model.

difficulties.pattern: Learners stop and restart sentences repeatedly to correct minor errors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent restarts; fragmented speech, often where accuracy has been the main criterion of success.
difficulties.response: Discuss which errors affect meaning and practise continuing past minor errors.

difficulties.pattern: Learners abandon a message when they cannot find a word.
difficulties.revealedBy: Messages left incomplete; avoidance of topics.
difficulties.response: Teach and practise paraphrase strategies in a supportive setting.

difficulties.pattern: Learners do not notice signs that a listener has not understood.
difficulties.revealedBy: Continuing with an explanation despite puzzled looks or questions.
difficulties.response: Practise recognising non-understanding signals and responding with reformulation markers.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to explain a concept without using its key term.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Clear paraphrase with appropriate reformulation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Some paraphrase with hesitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives up or relies on the term.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant from foundation to in-sessional level. At foundation level, emphasise compensatory strategies; for in-sessional students, focus on meaning-affecting errors in disciplinary speech.

guidance.summary: Segalowitz (2010) distinguishes cognitive fluency (the efficiency of underlying processing), utterance fluency (measurable features such as speed, pausing and repair) and perceived fluency (listeners' judgements). Skehan (1998) showed that pre-task planning and task design affect fluency, with trade-offs against accuracy and complexity. Formulaic sequences reduce online processing load (Wood, 2010), and repetition under time pressure, as in 4/3/2 (Nation & Newton, 2009), is a well-known fluency-development activity. Practice should aim at automatisation through repetition on familiar content, not simply more speaking.

activities.title: 4/3/2 on a research topic
learnerActions: Talk for 4 minutes to a partner about a topic from their field
Repeat the same talk to a new partner in 3 minutes
Repeat again to a third partner in 2 minutes
Reflect on what changed
activities.intendedInsight: Repetition under time pressure is intended to make delivery of familiar content smoother.
activities.rationale: The 4/3/2 activity is described by Nation and Newton (2009) as a fluency-development technique.

activities.title: Formula bank for presentations
learnerActions: Collect signposting and hedging formulas from lectures and presentations
Practise them as units until automatic
Use them in a short presentation
activities.intendedInsight: Formulaic language can free attention for content.
activities.rationale: Builds on Wood's (2010) account of formulaic sequences and fluency.

difficulties.pattern: 'Fluency means speaking fast.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Rushed speech that listeners find harder to follow.
difficulties.response: Explain fluency as smooth delivery with appropriate pausing, not speed.

difficulties.pattern: Learners memorise full scripts and freeze when they lose their place.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent delivery that breaks down entirely after a disruption.
difficulties.response: Practise from notes and with formulaic chunks rather than full scripts.

difficulties.pattern: Anxiety increases pausing and hesitation in front of an audience.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluency much better in pairs than in front of a group.
difficulties.response: Build up gradually from pairs to groups; use repetition to increase confidence.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to speak for 2 minutes on a familiar topic, then repeat after planning time.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Fluent in both, with pauses at boundaries.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves markedly with planning.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent mid-clause pauses even after planning.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant at all stages. For PGR students, fluency in conference presentations and vivas is important; formulaic language for presenting research can be targeted. For students who stammer, fluency work should not aim at eliminating disfluency: judge communicative effectiveness, allow extra time, and follow the student's own preferences and any specialist advice.

guidance.summary: Numbers, formulae and units are frequent in presentations across many disciplines, and errors can mislead listeners about findings. SI conventions (Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, 2019) govern unit names and symbols, while spoken conventions for formulae vary by discipline and region. Teach common patterns, the -teen/-ty contrast (relying mainly on the final syllable, because -teen stress shifts forward before a stressed noun) and confirmation strategies, and have learners practise with figures from their own fields.

activities.title: Read the table
learnerActions: Read aloud a table of results from their field
A partner writes down the figures
Compare and identify misheard figures
activities.intendedInsight: Listeners need numbers said clearly and sometimes confirmed.
activities.rationale: Tests intelligibility of spoken numbers directly.

activities.title: Say the formula
learnerActions: Practise saying common formulae and units from their field
Check conventions with a subject source
Record a short explanation of an equation
activities.intendedInsight: Formulae have conventional spoken forms.
activities.rationale: Practice-based activity; unit names follow SI conventions.

difficulties.pattern: Learners confuse -teen and -ty numbers.
difficulties.revealedBy: Listeners mishear figures such as 15 and 50.
difficulties.response: Practise the final-syllable contrast (/tiːn/ versus /ti/) in phrases such as fourteen students, where stress shift removes the stress cue, and confirm critical numbers (one five, fifteen).

difficulties.pattern: Learners read decimals and large numbers using conventions from their first language, for example decimal commas or different grouping of digits.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in spoken decimals and large numbers.
difficulties.response: Contrast conventions explicitly and practise English forms.

difficulties.pattern: Learners do not know how to read equations aloud.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hesitation or avoidance when explaining formulae.
difficulties.response: Teach conventional spoken forms for common operations.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to read aloud a slide with a table, a formula and a date range.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All figures accurate and intelligible.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most figures correct but some confusions or hesitations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent errors or avoidance.

guidance.contextNotes: Relevant from foundation level, especially for STEM and business pathways. PGT students presenting data need fluent control of statistics and units.
reviewNotes: The bibliography has no source on spoken number conventions; guidance is practice-based.

authorNotes: LIS/PRS overlap: coh.spoken-signposting has been merged into prs.signposting. lis.lecture-discourse-markers is the reception topic and no longer depends on prs.signposting, so the PRS author can make prs.signposting depend on it (recognition before production).

lis.accent-variation depends (soft) on idn.elf. The IDN author should not make idn.elf depend on lis.accent-variation; prn.intelligibility (an entry point here) is a safe soft prerequisite for idn.elf if one is wanted.

Gap: there is no receptive prosody topic (perceiving prominence, tone and pitch reset as cues in listening). Several LIS topics rely on prosodic cues, so I have used production topics (prn.prominence, prn.intonation) as soft prerequisites. A topic such as 'lis.prosodic-cues' would make these dependencies cleaner.
lis.listening-processes is largely teacher-facing conceptual knowledge; it could be merged into lis.metacognitive-listening as its 'task knowledge' component without loss.

Suggested outgoing edges for other strands: sem.questions-clarification and sem.building-on-others could take lis.multi-party-discussion as a soft prerequisite; syn.integrated-tasks and tst.integrated-test-tasks could take lis.main-points (and ntk.lecture-notes) as prerequisites.

Gap: listening to questions from an audience (the receptive side of prs.handling-questions and pub.viva) and listening in one-to-one supervision are not covered by any LIS topic; prg.office-hours and res.supervision may implicitly cover the latter.

Suggested outgoing edges for other strands: src.paraphrasing and src.summarising-passage could take ntk.notes-from-reading as a soft prerequisite; syn.synthesis-matrix could take ntk.note-formats; wpr.reading-to-write could take ntk.notes-from-reading; exm.revision-planning could take ntk.reviewing-notes. None of these SRC, SYN, WPR or EXM topics should be made prerequisites of NTK topics, or cycles may result.

Overlap: ntk.notes-from-reading overlaps with rds.annotation and inf.search-records; ntk.reviewing-notes overlaps with lrn.study-techniques; ntk.digital-notes overlaps with dig.file-management. Scope notes should make the NTK topics the place where note-specific practice is taught.
Gap: PGR literature note-making within reference managers (notes attached to records, tagging, annotation sync) is not clearly covered by either ntk.digital-notes or dig.reference-managers.

Suggested outgoing edges for other strands: prs.delivery-voice could take prn.thought-groups and prn.prominence as prerequisites; prs.signposting could take prn.intonation (soft); prs.research-presentations and prs.explaining-visuals could take prn.technical-terms and prn.numbers-aloud; sem.checking-understanding could take prn.repair. These PRS and SEM topics should not be made prerequisites of PRN topics.

Direction choices that other authors should respect to avoid cycles: prn.fluency depends on phr.spoken-academic-formulas; prn.numbers-aloud depends on num.number-expressions and num.mathematical-expression; prn.intonation depends on reg.spoken-vs-written; prn.repair depends on fun.defining and sta.code-glosses.
Overlap: prs.delivery-voice (pace, volume, pausing, emphasis) overlaps substantially with prn.thought-groups and prn.prominence; its scope note could be narrowed to presentation-specific delivery.
prn.intelligibility is an entry point; idn.elf and idn.standards-legitimacy could take it as a soft prerequisite.
Proposed reference thomson2018hvpt supports the HVPT activity in prn.segmental-priorities (review finding R2-41).
